title: Partners and rivals: why very different living beings trade, and why seedlings of one kind compete

summary.text: A grey-green patch on an old tree is a lichen: a fungus and an alga living as one body. Why do such different beings join up, while seedlings of one kind get in each other's way? In this lesson you will grow 4, 16 and 64 methi seeds in cups and study partners as trades.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a tree trunk with a grey-green leafy lichen and a zoom circle showing fungus threads around round green cells, on the right three cups of seedlings, one with four sturdy seedlings and one packed with thin tall ones.

intro.hook: Sixty-four methi seedlings in one cup all need the same light and water. A fungus and an alga inside a lichen need quite different things. Which of these two groups do you think gets along better, and why?
intro.text: Living beings affect each other in many ways. Some eat others. Some compete, which means they need the same thing and there is not enough for all. And some are partners: each gives the other something, and both live better. In this lesson you test competition yourself, with methi seeds in crowded and roomy cups. Then you look closely at three famous partnerships: bees and flowers, fungi and roots, and the lichens on rocks and trees. You find out what each partner gives and gets, and why partnerships are not always fair.
intro.art: A child looking closely at a cup crowded with thin methi seedlings on a window sill, with a piece of grey-green lichen (kalpasi from the spice box) lying on a steel plate beside the cup.

outcomes: I can tell mutualism, competition, parasitism and commensalism apart by asking who gains and who loses.
I can run a fair test on crowding, and use my results to explain what seedlings of one kind compete for.
I can explain a partnership as a trade: what each partner gives, what each gets, and why each cannot easily get it alone.
I can describe how a root and a fungus trade sugar for minerals, and how each keeps the trade fair.
I can explain what a lichen is, how the partners live as one body, and what lichens tell us about the air.
I can give examples of cheating in partnerships, and explain why the same two beings can be partners in one place and not in another.
I can say what scientists agree on about partnerships and what they still argue about.

terms.meaning: Anything a living being needs and uses up, such as light, water, minerals, food or space.
terms.example: The water in a cup of soil is a resource. When 64 seedlings share it, each seedling gets less.
terms.art: A cup of soil seen from the side with many seedling roots all reaching for the same few drops of water.

terms.meaning: What happens when living beings need the same resource and there is not enough for all of them. Each one gets less than they would alone.
terms.example: Two mango seedlings that sprout side by side compete for light. The taller one shades the other.
terms.art: Two young seedlings side by side, the taller one's leaf casting a shadow over the shorter one.

terms.meaning: Two different kinds of living beings living closely together for a long time. The word only says they live together. It does not say whether this helps or harms them.
terms.example: A lichen is a symbiosis of a fungus and an alga. A tapeworm in a gut is also a symbiosis.
terms.art: Two different living beings drawn as two differently coloured shapes fitted closely together like puzzle pieces.

terms.meaning: A symbiosis in which both partners gain more than they lose.
terms.example: A bee gets nectar from a flower, and the flower gets her pollen carried to another flower. Both gain.
terms.art: A honeybee on a yellow pumpkin flower with pollen grains on her body, and a small plus sign beside each.

terms.meaning: A symbiosis in which one being gains and the other is harmed. The one who gains is called a parasite and the one harmed is called the host.
terms.example: A head louse drinks a person's blood. The louse gains and the person loses.
terms.art: A tick on the ear of a street dog, with a plus sign by the tick and a minus sign by the dog.

terms.meaning: A symbiosis in which one being gains and the other is neither helped nor harmed, as far as we can tell.
terms.example: An orchid growing on a branch of a jackfruit tree gets a place in the light. The tree seems to lose nothing.
terms.art: An orchid with pink flowers growing on a thick jackfruit branch high above the ground.

terms.meaning: A sweet liquid that many flowers make. It is mostly water with sugars dissolved in it. Flowers make it as payment for visitors.
terms.example: A sunbird pushes her curved beak into a hibiscus flower to drink the nectar at the bottom.
terms.art: A purple sunbird with her beak deep in a red hibiscus flower, and a drop of nectar shown at the base of the flower.

terms.meaning: Taking nectar through a hole bitten in the side of a flower, without touching the pollen.
terms.example: A big black carpenter bee bites a hole at the base of a long flower and drinks. She carries no pollen away.
terms.art: A large black carpenter bee on the outside of a tube-shaped flower, biting a small hole near its base.

terms.meaning: One thread of a fungus. The body of a fungus is made of very many of these threads. The plural is hyphae.
terms.example: The white fluff on mouldy bread is a mass of hyphae. Each thread is far thinner than a hair.
terms.art: A zoom circle on a patch of white bread mould showing the mould as a tangle of fine branching threads.

terms.meaning: A partnership between a fungus and the roots of a plant. The word means 'fungus-root'. The plural is mycorrhizae.
terms.example: The roots of a mango tree are joined to fungi in the soil. The fungi bring minerals, and the tree gives sugar.
terms.art: A tree root underground with fine white fungal threads spreading from it far into the soil.

terms.meaning: A simple green living being who makes food from sunlight, air and water, as plants do, but has no roots, stems or leaves. The plural is algae.
terms.example: The green film on a damp bathroom wall or a water tank is made of algae.
terms.art: A zoom circle on a green film on a damp wall showing many small round green cells.

terms.meaning: A fungus and an alga, or a fungus and a food-making bacterium, living together as one body. The lichen looks like neither partner alone.
terms.example: Kalpasi, the 'stone flower' in Chettinad masala, is a dried lichen.
terms.art: A grey-green leafy lichen with a black underside lying on a steel plate next to a few whole spices.

terms.meaning: The way a plant grows a longer, thinner stem when they sense other plants close by. It lifts their leaves towards the light.
terms.example: Methi sown thickly in a tray grows tall and thin. Each seedling is trying to get above the others.
terms.art: A tray of thickly sown seedlings, all tall and thin, beside one short sturdy seedling in a pot of their own.

terms.meaning: A being who takes what a partner offers but gives little or nothing back. Scientists use the word without blame.
terms.example: Some orchids make no nectar at all. Bees visit, find nothing and still carry the pollen away.
terms.art: A bee backing out of an orchid flower with a pollen packet stuck to her back and a puzzled look, the flower's nectar cup empty.

terms.meaning: A living being whose presence or absence tells us about the place, such as how clean the air is.
terms.example: Where bushy lichens hang from tree branches, the air is usually clean.
terms.art: A hill-station tree branch with pale bushy lichens hanging from it under a clear sky.

explanations.concept: Four ways of living together: who gains and who loses?
explanations.definition: When two kinds of living beings affect each other, ask of each one: do they gain, lose, or neither? If both gain, it is mutualism. If both lose, it is competition. If one gains and one loses, it is parasitism or predation. If one gains and the other is not affected, it is commensalism.
explanations.description: Scientists sort the ways living beings affect each other by results, not by intentions. A bee does not visit a flower to be helpful. She visits to feed herself and her hive. But the result is that both she and the plant gain, so this is mutualism. The word symbiosis is often used to mean a happy partnership. In science it only means living closely together, and that can help or harm. These four names are useful, but real pairs do not always stay in one box. Later cards show that the same two beings can be partners in one place and not in another.
examples: Both gain: a sunbird drinks nectar from a coral tree flower and carries pollen to the next tree.
Both lose: two tomato plants in one small pot each get less water and fewer minerals than one plant alone would.
One gains and one loses: a mosquito drinks your blood.
One gains and the other is not affected: a cattle egret eats the insects that a grazing buffalo stirs up from the grass.
explanations.art: A table with four rows, each showing two beings with a plus, minus or zero beside each: bee and flower, two crowded seedlings, mosquito and arm, egret and buffalo.

explanations.concept: Competition is strongest between those who are most alike
explanations.definition: Competition happens when living beings need the same resource and there is not enough for all. Nobody has to fight. Each one simply uses up some of what the others need.
explanations.description: In the Crowded Cup Test, no seedling attacks another. Each root takes water, and that water is no longer there for the root beside it. Why are the strongest competitors usually members of the same kind? Because they need exactly the same things, at the same depth in the soil, at the same time of day. Charles Darwin wrote in 1859 that the struggle for life is most severe between individuals of the same species. In 1934 the Russian scientist Georgy Gause tested this with two kinds of tiny one-celled pond animals called Paramecium. Both kinds ate the same bacteria. Each kind lived well alone. Together in one tube, one kind slowly died out. But a third kind, who fed mostly on yeast instead, could live alongside. In nature, kinds that live side by side usually differ a little in what they use.
examples: In the Crowded Cup Test, 64 methi seedlings share the same water as 4 seedlings in the next cup.
Farmers pull out extra seedlings so that the ones left have room. This is called thinning.
In a paddy field, weeds and rice compete for light, water and minerals. That is why farmers weed.
A bulbul and a sunbird can feed in the same tree, because one eats fruit and the other drinks nectar.
explanations.art: Two test tubes: in the first, two kinds of slipper-shaped one-celled animals with one kind fading away, in the second, two kinds living together because one feeds at the top and one at the bottom.

explanations.concept: How a seedling knows they have neighbours
explanations.definition: A plant senses nearby plants by the colour of the light that reaches them. Then they grow a longer, thinner stem. This is called shade avoidance.
explanations.description: Why are crowded seedlings often taller, when they have less of everything? Green leaves soak up red light for making food. A kind of light called far-red, which our eyes can hardly see, passes through leaves or bounces off them. So light that has met other leaves has less red in it and more far-red. A seedling has sensors in their cells that compare the two. When far-red is high, the seedling senses neighbours, even before being shaded. They put their food into a longer stem instead of thicker stems and bigger leaves. In a crowd this is a risky choice. Every neighbour does the same, so nobody gets ahead, and all end up thin and easy to knock over.
examples: Methi or mustard grown thickly for eating as small greens is tall, thin and pale near the bottom.
A seedling growing alone in a pot is shorter and has a thicker stem.
Trees planted close together in a plantation grow tall, straight trunks with few low branches.

perspectives.explanation: They describe shade avoidance as a response set off by light sensors, and prefer not to use the word 'choose'.
They point out that the plant takes in information, weighs it against other signals such as dryness, and then grows one way or another. They call that a decision.

explanations.art: A side view of crowded seedlings with red light arrows being soaked up by the upper leaves and far-red arrows passing down to a small seedling underneath, whose stem is stretching.

explanations.definition: In a mutualism, each partner gives something that costs them little and gets something they could not easily get alone.
explanations.description: Think about why a flower and a bee are good partners. A plant can make sugar from sunlight, air and water, so sugar is cheap for a plant. But a plant cannot walk to another plant to carry pollen. A bee can fly, so carrying pollen is cheap for a bee. But a bee cannot make sugar. Each has what the other lacks. This is true of every partnership in this lesson. The two partners are very different kinds of living beings, and the difference is what gives them something to exchange. Every trade also has a cost. Nectar uses sugar the plant could have used to grow. So each partner does best by giving as little as they can and getting as much as they can. That is why partnerships are never perfectly fair.
examples: Flower and bee: the flower gives sugar, and the bee gives transport for pollen.
Root and fungus: the plant gives sugar, and the fungus gives minerals and water from far-off soil.
Lichen: the alga gives sugar, and the fungus gives a body that holds water and grips the rock.

A tree called Humboldtia brunonis in the Western Ghats gives ants hollow stems to live in and nectar to drink. Renee Borges and her team at the Indian Institute of Science found that one kind of ant drives leaf-eaters off the tree.
explanations.art: A weighing balance with a drop of nectar on one pan and a pollen grain with tiny wings on the other, a flower beside one pan and a bee beside the other.

explanations.concept: Bees and flowers: payment, advertising and cheating
explanations.definition: Pollination by animals is a trade of food for transport. The flower pays with nectar or pollen, and the visitor carries pollen to another flower of the same kind.
explanations.description: About 9 of every 10 kinds of flowering plants have their pollen carried by animals: bees, flies, butterflies, moths, birds and bats. A flower's colour and smell are advertisements. They tell a visitor where the payment is. The shape of the flower makes the visitor brush against the pollen on the way to the nectar. Both sides can cheat. A carpenter bee may bite a hole in the side of a long flower and drink without touching the pollen. This is nectar robbing. Flowers cheat too. Many orchids make no nectar, and some look or smell like food to trick insects into visiting. So why does the trade not break down? Because cheating has limits. A flower that never pays is soon avoided by bees who learn. A plant robbed too often makes few seeds.
examples: In Kerala, tiny stingless bees are among the main pollinators of sponge gourd and ash gourd flowers.
The Indian hive bee and the rock bee visit mustard, coconut, mango and coffee flowers.
Rice, wheat and maize need no animal. Their pollen is carried by wind, or falls within the same flower.
About 3 in 4 of the world's main food crops give more fruit or seed when animals pollinate them.
explanations.art: A cut-away tube-shaped flower with a bee crawling in past the pollen to reach nectar at the bottom, and a carpenter bee outside biting a hole near the base.

explanations.concept: Fungi and roots: the trade under the ground
explanations.definition: A mycorrhiza is a partnership between a fungus and a plant root. The plant gives the fungus sugar. The fungus gives the plant minerals and water gathered from soil that the root cannot reach.
explanations.description: A plant makes sugar in their leaves, but needs minerals from the soil. One of the most important is phosphate, which every cell needs to build new parts. Phosphate sticks to soil grains and hardly moves. A root soon uses up the phosphate right next to it. Fungal hyphae are many times thinner than the finest root, so they can enter gaps in the soil that no root can enter. They also spread far beyond the root. A fungus, however, cannot make sugar, because fungi have no green food-making parts. So the two trade. The hyphae grow into the root and meet the root cells there. More than 8 of every 10 kinds of land plants have fungus partners like this. A few families do not, and the mustard and cabbage family is one. In 2011 Toby Kiers and her team traced the trade with marked atoms. They found that plants sent more sugar to fungi that gave more phosphate. Fungi sent more phosphate to roots that gave more sugar.
examples: Mango, coconut, coffee, teak, tomato and ragi all have fungus partners on their roots.
Mustard, cabbage, cauliflower and radish belong to a family that grows without them.
The name mycorrhiza was given by the German scientist Albert Bernhard Frank in 1885.
An orchid seed is as fine as dust and carries almost no food. The seed can grow only after a fungus begins to feed them.
explanations.art: A cut-away of soil showing a root with a zone of used-up soil around it, and fine fungal threads reaching from inside the root out through the zone into fresh soil, with arrows marked sugar going out and phosphate coming in.

explanations.concept: Lichens: two beings in one body
explanations.definition: A lichen is a fungus living together with an alga, or with a food-making bacterium, as a single body. The fungus makes most of the body. The green partner makes the food.
explanations.description: Cut across a leafy lichen and look with a microscope. On top is a skin of tightly packed hyphae. Under it lies a thin green layer of algae, each cell wrapped in hyphae. Below is a loose layer of hyphae with air spaces, and then a lower skin with small threads that grip the bark or rock. The alga makes sugar from sunlight, and some of this sugar passes to the fungus. The fungus gives the alga a home that holds water, shades them from harsh sun and grips a surface. A lichen has no roots and no waxy skin. They take in water and minerals from rain, mist and dust over their whole surface. When the air is dry, the lichen dries out and stops working. When rain comes, they start again within minutes. This is how lichens live on bare rock, on tree bark and in deserts and snow, where neither partner could easily live alone. It is also why dirty air harms them. They soak up whatever the rain carries.
examples: More than 3,000 kinds of lichen have been recorded in India.
Kalpasi or dagad phool, the 'stone flower' used in Chettinad and Maharashtrian cooking, is a dried leafy lichen.
Most lichens grow only a few millimetres wider in a year, so a patch as wide as your palm may be older than you.
In 2005, two kinds of lichen were carried outside a spacecraft for about 15 days. Back on Earth, most of their cells were alive.
explanations.art: A cross-section of a leafy lichen in four labelled layers: upper skin of packed threads, green layer of round algal cells wrapped in threads, loose threads with air spaces, lower skin with gripping threads on bark.

explanations.concept: Is the alga in a lichen a partner or a captive?
explanations.description: For most of the last 150 years, books have called the lichen a fair partnership. But the two sides are not in the same position, and scientists read the evidence in different ways.
examples: Many of the algae found in lichens can also be found living on their own, on bark and damp walls.
Most lichen fungi have never been found living without their green partner.
In 2016 Toby Spribille and his team found a second fungus, a kind of yeast, in the skin of many lichens. What the yeast does is still being studied.

perspectives.explanation: Inside the lichen, the alga lives in places where they would dry out or burn in the sun alone. Lichens cover bare rock where no free alga grows. So the alga gains a far wider world.

perspectives.who: Scientists who call it controlled parasitism
perspectives.explanation: The fungus takes much of the sugar the alga makes, and the alga grows more slowly inside the lichen than outside. The fungus needs the alga far more than the alga needs the fungus. Some say the fungus farms the alga, as people farm crops.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say the question is too simple
perspectives.explanation: A lichen may hold several kinds of fungi, algae and bacteria. They see a lichen as a small community, with gains and losses that change with the weather.

explanations.art: A round green algal cell wrapped in fungal threads, with two thought bubbles above it, one showing a safe house and one showing a cage.

explanations.definition: Whether a partnership helps or harms a partner depends on the conditions. The same fungus can help a plant in poor soil and cost the plant more than they give in rich soil.
explanations.description: A trade is only worth making if you need what the other side sells. In soil with little phosphate, a plant gains a lot from a fungus partner. In a field given plenty of fertiliser, the plant can get phosphate easily through their own roots. The fungus still takes sugar. Now the plant pays and gets little back, and may grow slightly less than a plant with no fungus. In 1997 Nancy Johnson and two other scientists described this as a line with mutualism at one end and parasitism at the other. A partnership can slide along the line as conditions change. Corals show the same thing. Tiny algae live inside the coral animal and feed them. When the sea stays a degree or two warmer than usual, the trade breaks down. The coral loses the algae, turns white, and may starve.
examples: Plants in heavily fertilised soil often have fewer fungus partners on their roots.
In 2016 a long hot spell in the sea turned many corals white in the Gulf of Mannar, off Tamil Nadu.
A bee who usually pollinates a flower properly may rob the same kind of flower when a hole is already there.
explanations.art: A long line with the word mutualism at the left end and parasitism at the right, and a plant-with-fungus marker sliding along it as a bag of fertiliser is poured on the soil.

explanations.concept: From meeting to merging: how close can partners become?
explanations.definition: Partners can be joined loosely or tightly. At the loosest, they meet for a few seconds. At the tightest, one lives inside the cells of the other and neither can ever live alone again.
explanations.description: A bee and a flower meet for seconds and part. A root and a fungus live joined, but each still has their own body. In a lichen, the two build one body together. The closest partnership of all is inside your own cells. Each of your cells holds tiny parts called mitochondria, which release energy from food. They have their own genes, quite unlike the genes in the rest of the cell. In 1967 the American scientist Lynn Margulis argued that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria. Long ago they began living inside larger cells and never left. The green food-making parts in plant cells began the same way. Her paper was turned down by about fifteen journals before one printed it. Later, studies of genes showed that she was right about both. So every plant and every animal, including you, is built from cells that began as a partnership.
examples: Seconds: a butterfly on a lantana flower.
A lifetime, with two bodies: a banyan root and their fungi.
One body: a lichen on a rock.
One cell: the mitochondria inside every cell of your body.
explanations.art: Four steps drawn like a ladder: a bee touching a flower, a root wrapped in fungal threads, a lichen, and a cell with small bean-shaped mitochondria inside.

explanations.concept: Do trees share food through fungi?
explanations.description: One fungus can be joined to the roots of several trees at once. In 1997 the Canadian forester Suzanne Simard marked carbon atoms in birch and fir seedlings growing together. Some marked carbon from one seedling turned up in the other. Many books and films now say that forest trees feed and warn each other through a 'wood wide web' of fungi. Scientists agree on less than that.
examples: Shared fungal threads between trees are real, and carbon can move across them.
The name 'wood wide web' came from the journal that printed the 1997 study, not from Simard.
In 2023 three scientists checked more than 1,500 papers and found that many repeated claims went beyond the tests.

perspectives.who: Suzanne Simard and scientists who work with her
perspectives.explanation: They say the tests show that large trees pass carbon to shaded seedlings through shared fungi, and that this helps the seedlings live. In 2025 they answered their critics and stood by this view.

perspectives.who: Justine Karst, Melanie Jones and Jason Hoeksema
perspectives.explanation: They wrote in 2023 that the evidence from real forests is thin. The amounts of carbon are small, and it could have moved through the soil. They found that claims without good evidence had become much more common in science papers.

perspectives.who: Scientists who look at it from the fungus's side
perspectives.explanation: They ask why a fungus would carry food from one tree to another for nothing. The fungus may simply be moving food to where the fungus themself needs it.

explanations.art: Two trees of different kinds, a big one in sunlight and a small one in shade, with fungal threads joining their roots underground and a question mark on the arrow between them.

explanations.definition: The first land plants already had fungus partners. Lichens and fungi also helped to make the first soils.
explanations.description: The early land was bare rock, sand and mud. The first small plants had no real roots. In Scotland there is a rock called the Rhynie chert, which holds plants turned to stone more than 400 million years ago. In 1994 scientists found fungi inside the cells of one of these plants. The fungi had the same small tree-like shape that mycorrhizal fungi make inside root cells today. So the trade of sugar for minerals is at least that old. Lichens are among the first living beings to settle on bare rock, even today. They hold water against the rock, and their acids slowly wear the rock away. Dust and dead lichen pieces collect, mosses follow, and soil begins.
examples: On a fresh lava flow or a new stone wall, lichens are often the first to arrive.
A coral reef is rock built by coral animals, who are fed by the algae living inside them.
Coconut palms growing in poor, sandy soil have root fungi that help them find scarce minerals.
explanations.art: A bare grey rock in four stages from left to right: bare, with lichen crusts, with moss and a little soil, with small plants growing.

agreed.text: Living beings who need the same scarce resource reduce each other's growth, and this is strongest between members of the same kind.
agreed.evidence: Crowding tests with seedlings, like your Crowded Cup Test, give this result again and again. Gause's tests of 1934 showed it with one-celled animals.

agreed.text: In a mutualism, both partners gain more than they lose, and each acts for their own benefit.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measure growth and number of young with and without the partner. Flowers kept from pollinators make fewer seeds, and bees without flowers starve.

agreed.text: Most land plants trade sugar for minerals with fungi on their roots.
agreed.evidence: Hyphae can be seen inside root cells with a microscope. Marked carbon and phosphorus atoms have been followed from one partner to the other.

agreed.text: A lichen is a fungus living with one or more food-making partners as one body.
agreed.evidence: Simon Schwendener proposed this in 1867. Since then the partners have been separated, grown apart and identified by their genes.

agreed.text: Partnerships can break down or turn harmful when conditions change.
agreed.evidence: Corals lose their algae in water that stays too warm. Plants in heavily fertilised soil can grow less with root fungi than without.

agreed.text: Mitochondria, and the green food-making parts of plant cells, began as free-living bacteria.
agreed.evidence: They have their own genes, which are most like the genes of certain bacteria, and they divide on their own inside the cell.

challenging.claim: Nature is a fight, and every living being is against every other.
challenging.who: Thomas Huxley wrote in 1888 that the animal world is on about the level of a gladiators' show. Many people still picture nature this way.
challenging.for: Competition is real. In the Crowded Cup Test, more seedlings meant less for each. Predators kill, and most young die.
challenging.against: Peter Kropotkin answered Huxley in a set of articles, printed as the book Mutual Aid in 1902. He had watched animals in Siberia and saw them helping each other through hard winters far more than fighting. Today we know that most plants depend on fungi, most flowers on animals, and every animal on microbes.
challenging.context: This card is about the old belief that nature is only a struggle of each against all.

challenging.claim: Nature is a harmony in which everyone helps everyone.
challenging.who: A common belief, often found in books and films about forests
challenging.for: Partnerships are everywhere, and no plant or animal lives without them.
challenging.against: Partners do not help out of kindness. Each gives as little as they can for what they get. Bees rob flowers, orchids trick bees, and a root fungus can become a burden in rich soil. Both the 'fight' picture and the 'harmony' picture leave out half of what happens.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that living beings in nature all help each other.

challenging.claim: Old trees feed young trees through fungal threads.
challenging.who: Suzanne Simard and others, and many popular books and films
challenging.for: Fungi do join the roots of different trees, and marked carbon has moved between seedlings in tests.
challenging.against: A 2023 review found that the amounts are small and that few tests were done in real forests. The carbon may travel through soil, not only through fungi. Nobody has shown that a tree sends food to another tree on purpose.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea of a 'wood wide web', in which trees share food through fungi.

challenging.claim: A lichen is not a partnership. It is a fungus that farms algae.
challenging.for: The fungus takes much of the alga's sugar, and the alga grows more slowly inside the lichen. Most lichen fungi cannot live alone, but many of the algae can.
challenging.against: Inside a lichen, algae live on bare rock and dry bark where they could not survive alone. If we count how many places a being can live, the alga gains too.
challenging.context: This card is about whether both partners in a lichen really gain.

challenging.claim: Humans stand outside these partnerships and only watch them.
challenging.who: A common way of speaking, as if nature were somewhere else
challenging.for: People can live in cities, far from forests, and buy food in shops.
challenging.against: About 3 in 4 of our main food crops give more when animals pollinate them. Most crops depend on root fungi. Microbes in our gut digest parts of our food for us. And each of our cells runs on mitochondria that were once bacteria. Humans are animals, and we live inside partnerships like every other animal.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that people are separate from nature's partnerships.

big_questions.q: If a bee visits a flower only to feed herself, is she helping the flower?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between what someone means to do and what their action does. Scientists sort partnerships by results. Would you?

big_questions.q: Is a lichen one living being or two?
big_questions.hint: The fungus and the alga have different genes and can sometimes be grown apart. But apart, neither looks like a lichen. What makes something 'one'?

big_questions.q: Your cells run on mitochondria that were once free bacteria. Are you one being or a partnership?
big_questions.hint: You cannot live without them, and they cannot live without you. Does it matter that the joining happened long ago?

big_questions.q: Why are partners usually so different from each other, while rivals are so alike?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one needs and what each one can make. What could two methi seedlings possibly give each other?

big_questions.q: Can a trade be good for both sides and still be unfair?
big_questions.hint: The alga in a lichen may gain a home and lose most of their sugar. Who decides what is fair, when the partners cannot talk it over?

big_questions.q: Has cooperation or competition done more to shape life on Earth?
big_questions.hint: Competition explains why crowded seedlings grow thin. Cooperation explains lichens, flowers and your own cells. Scientists still argue about which matters more.

story.title: The Dust Seeds
story.note: This story is imagined. The science in it is real. An orchid seed has no food store, and in the wild the seed can grow only when a fungus enters and feeds them. The French scientist Noël Bernard found this in 1899. Kaveri's bark test is made up, and orchids are slow, so a real test could take longer than hers. Scientists are still working out whether, and how much, a grown orchid gives back to the fungus.
text: The orchid on the old jackfruit tree flowered every April, in a hanging spray of pink as long as Kaveri's arm. Nobody had planted her. She sat in the fork of the tree, high above the coffee bushes, and her grey roots held the bark like fingers.

In June, after the flowers, one green pod was left. Kaveri, who was ten, watched that pod all through the first rains. Her school in Madikeri was making a garden, and she had promised to bring an orchid she had grown herself.
'From seed,' she told her brother Muthu, who was seven. 'Not a piece broken off. That would be cheating.'

In September the pod turned yellow and split. Kaveri climbed the ladder with a sheet of white paper and tapped the pod. What fell out was not seeds as she knew seeds. It was dust, pale brown and finer than ragi flour. One breath sent half of it over the edge of the paper.
'That's all?' said Muthu.
'That is thousands,' said Kaveri. 'Look how many.'

She did it properly. She filled a clay pot with the dark soil from under the coffee bushes, the best soil on the estate. She sprinkled the dust, watered it with a spoon, and set the pot where the morning sun came in. Beans came up in that soil in four days. She gave the dust two weeks, and then four.
Nothing came up. Not one green point.
She tried again on wet cotton in a steel plate, the way she sprouted ragi. In a week the cotton had grown a grey fur of mould, and the dust lay under the mould, unchanged.
'They are dead seeds,' said Muthu.

'They are not dead. The pod was fresh.' But she was not sure. She took their father's lens, the one he used for looking at coffee beans, and put a pinch of the dust under it. Each seed was a tiny pale bag, as thin as a thread, with one dark speck in the middle. That was all.

She fetched a bean from the kitchen and split the bean with her thumbnail. Inside were two fat halves, hard and cream-coloured, and tucked between them was a baby plant no bigger than a comma. She had drawn this in Class 3. The fat halves were the food. The baby plant lived on them until the first leaves could work.
She looked at the dust again. A speck in a bag. No fat halves. Nothing packed for the journey.
'Muthu,' she said slowly. 'A bean seed carries tiffin. This one carries nothing at all.'
'Then how does any orchid ever grow?'
Kaveri did not know. That was the trouble. The tree was the proof that they did grow, and the pot was the proof that they did not.

The rain went on. One Saturday in October she climbed the ladder only to look at the mother plant, because she was tired of looking at the pot. The old roots ran down the bark in grey ropes. Moss grew between them, and the bark there was dark and soft and always damp.
And among the roots, pressed against the bark, were small green beads. She counted eleven. Each was the size of a mustard seed. Two of them had a single leaf, thinner than a grain of rice.

She held her breath so as not to blow them away. Then she searched the rest of the trunk, hand over hand. On the far side, where the bark was clean and dry, there was not one. On the branch above there were none. In her pot of the best soil on the estate there were none. They were only here, in the old roots of the mother, where some of the dust must have drifted when the pod split.
'The same seeds,' she said to Muthu, at the foot of the ladder. 'The same rain. They grew there and not here. So something is there that is not here.'
'What?'
'I can't see what. But a seed with no tiffin is being fed. Someone who lives on that bark is feeding them.'

She did not leave it at guessing. With her father's help she cut a piece of dead bark from under the orchid, as big as her hand, with old roots and moss still on it. She tied it with coir string to a branch of the mango tree by the house. Beside it she tied a second piece, clean bark from the far side of the jackfruit. Onto both she shook the last of the dust from the paper. Then she wrote the date in her notebook, and under the date: Old bark. Clean bark. Same seeds. Same branch. Wait.
Waiting was the hard part. The rains ended. The coffee ripened red and was picked. In January there was nothing on the clean bark. On the old bark there were five green beads.
Kaveri looked at them for a long time.
'So who is feeding them?' asked Muthu. 'And why? Do they get anything back?'
'I don't know yet,' said Kaveri. 'Maybe the orchid pays later, when she has leaves of her own. Maybe she never pays.' She closed the notebook. 'That is the next thing to find out.'
In June she carried the piece of old bark to school in a tiffin box lined with damp moss. Each green bead had one leaf showing.
story.epiphany: For the parent: an orchid seed carries no food, so the seed cannot start growing alone. A fungus that lives on the old bark and roots enters the seed and feeds them. That is why the seeds grew only where their partner already lived, and not in the best soil on the estate.
ask: Kaveri's seeds had water, light and good soil. What were they still missing?
She tied up two pieces of bark, not one. Why did she need the clean piece?
A bean seed carries food and an orchid seed does not. What can an orchid plant do because her seeds are so light?
Muthu asked whether the feeder gets anything back. How could a scientist find out?
Where else in this lesson does a living being depend on a partner right from the start of life?

A girl's hand tapping a split yellow pod over a sheet of white paper, with fine brown dust falling out.
A clay pot of dark soil with nothing growing, beside a steel plate of cotton covered in grey mould.

games.title: Partner, Rival or Robber?
games.context: This is a card game about telling partnerships from competition and from one-sided gains. Each card describes two living beings. You say who gains and who loses, and give the reason.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A sunbird drinks nectar from a hibiscus flower. Pollen sticks to her head, and she carries it to the next flower.
items.b: Both gain. The bird gets food and the plant gets pollen carried. This is mutualism.

items.f: Two neem seedlings sprout in the same crack in a wall.
items.b: Both lose. They need the same water and there is little of it. This is competition.

items.f: A carpenter bee bites a hole in the side of a long flower and drinks the nectar. She does not touch the pollen.
items.b: The bee gains and the plant loses. The plant paid nectar and got no pollen carried. This is nectar robbing.

items.f: A fungus in the soil joins the roots of a mango tree. The fungus brings minerals and gets sugar.
items.b: Both gain. Each gets what they cannot easily get alone. This is mutualism, called a mycorrhiza.

items.f: A head louse lives on a child's scalp and drinks blood.
items.b: The louse gains and the child loses. This is parasitism.

items.f: An orchid grows on a branch of a jackfruit tree. Her roots hold the bark but take nothing from the tree.
items.b: The orchid gains a place in the light. The tree neither gains nor loses. This is commensalism.

items.f: A fungus and an alga live as one body, a lichen, on a bare rock.
items.b: Usually counted as both gain. The fungus gets sugar and the alga gets a damp home. Scientists still argue about how much the alga gains.

items.f: Weeds come up thickly among young paddy plants.
items.b: Both lose. The weeds and the paddy need the same light, water and minerals. This is competition.

items.f: A cattle egret walks beside a grazing buffalo and eats the insects that fly up.
items.b: The egret gains easy food. The buffalo neither gains nor loses much. This is commensalism.

items.f: An orchid flower makes no nectar but looks like a flower that does. A bee visits, finds nothing, and leaves with pollen on her back.
items.b: The orchid gains and the bee loses time and effort. The orchid is a cheater.

items.f: Ants live in the hollow stems of a tree in the Western Ghats and drink the tree's nectar. They drive leaf-eating insects away.
items.b: Both gain. The ants get a home and food, and the tree keeps more leaves. This is mutualism.

items.f: Two crows find one vada on a window sill.
items.b: Both lose. Each gets less than they would alone. This is competition.

items.f: The yellow threads of a dodder plant wind around a hedge and push into the stems to take sap.
items.b: The dodder gains and the hedge loses. This is parasitism. Dodder has no green leaves of their own.

items.f: Tiny algae live inside a coral animal. The algae make sugar in sunlight, and the coral gives them a safe home.
items.b: Both gain. This is mutualism. If the sea stays too warm, the partnership breaks down.

items.f: Bacteria live in small lumps on the roots of a tur dal plant. They take nitrogen from the air and get sugar from the plant.
items.b: Both gain. The plant gets nitrogen in a form they can use, and the bacteria get food. This is mutualism.

items.f: A mosquito lands on your arm and drinks blood.
items.b: The mosquito gains and you lose. A female mosquito needs blood to make her eggs.

items.f: A small tree frog rests through the day inside the rolled leaf of a banana plant.
items.b: The frog gains shade and safety. The banana plant neither gains nor loses. This is commensalism.

items.f: Sixty-four methi seedlings grow in one small cup.
items.b: All lose. They share the same light, water and minerals. This is competition between members of one kind.

items.f: Bacteria in a cow's stomach break down the tough parts of grass. The cow cannot digest these parts alone.
items.b: Both gain. The bacteria get a warm home and food, and the cow gets food from grass. This is mutualism.

items.f: A clownfish lives among the stinging arms of a sea anemone. The fish is safe there and chases away fish who nibble the anemone.
items.b: Both gain. The fish gets shelter and the anemone gets a guard. This is mutualism.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, question side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say what happens to each of the two beings: gains, loses, or neither. Give a reason.
Turn the card over. Score 1 point if you were right about both beings.
Score 1 more point if you can name what each one gives or uses up.
If you scored, keep the card. If not, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
Stop when every card has been read once. The player with the most points wins. Playing alone: note your score, play again another day and try to beat it.

ask.q: On the cards where both gain, are the two beings alike or very different?
good: Very different: a bird and a plant, a fungus and a tree, a fish and an anemone.
On the cards where both lose, they are often the same kind.

flow.parent: A right answer needs a reason. The lichen card has no single right answer. Accept 'both gain' or 'the fungus gains more', if a reason is given.
flow.context: This is the main step of Partner, Rival or Robber? Here you play through the cards and score.

flow.kid: Sort the cards into four piles by result. Look at 'both gain' and 'both lose'. What is different about the pairs?

check.q: In which pair are the two beings most likely to compete?
options: A bee and a mustard flower
Two mustard plants in one pot
A fungus and a tree root
A coral and the algae inside
check.why: Two mustard plants need exactly the same things from the same pot, so each leaves less for the other. If you chose a pair of very different beings, look again at what each one needs. They need different things, so they have something to exchange.

flow.context: This is the last step of Partner, Rival or Robber? Here you sort the cards and look for a pattern.

games.title: Pay or Cheat? A game for a flower and a bee
games.context: This is a game for two about why partners do not always play fair, and what stops them cheating. One player is a flower and the other is a bee. Each round, each of you secretly chooses to play fair or to cheat.

Flower pays, bee robs: the flower gives 1 and takes nothing. The bee gives nothing and takes 3.
Flower is empty, bee carries pollen: the flower gives nothing and takes 3. The bee gives 1 and takes nothing.
Flower is empty, bee robs: nobody gives and nobody takes.

rules: You need 70 dry chana or beans, a bowl and one coin for each player. One player is the flower and one is the bee. Each takes 10 chana. Put the other 50 in the bowl. The bowl is the bank.
Each round, hide your coin under your hand. Heads up means 'I play fair'. Tails up means 'I cheat'.
A fair flower fills the nectar: she pays 1 chana into the bank. A fair bee carries the pollen: she pays 1 chana into the bank. A cheater pays nothing.
Lift your hands together. If the flower paid, the bee takes 3 chana from the bank. If the bee carried pollen, the flower takes 3 chana from the bank.
Game 1 is 8 rounds. Write each round on the score sheet. Count your chana at the end.

Game 2 is 8 more rounds, starting again with 10 chana each. There is one new rule. If your partner cheated in the last round, you may say 'No visit' before the coins are hidden. Then nobody pays or takes in that round.
The winner is the player with the most chana over both games. Also add up what the two of you made together in each game, and compare.

setup.caption: 3. Pay and take your chana. Write the round on the score sheet.

flow.do: 1. Count out 10 chana for each player and 50 for the bank. 2. Read the four result cards aloud. 3. Play one practice round with the coins showing.
flow.say: The flower pays with nectar. The bee pays with the work of carrying pollen. Each of us can pay, or cheat and pay nothing.
flow.kid: Take 10 chana each. Put 50 in the bowl. Read the four result cards. Play one practice round.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pay or Cheat? Here you set up the chana and learn what each choice costs and earns.

flow.do: 1. Play the first game for 8 rounds. 2. Write each round on the score sheet. 3. Count each player's chana and add the two totals.
flow.say: Hide your coin. Ready? Lift. Let us see what each of us gets this round.
flow.kid: Play 8 rounds. Hide your coin, then lift your hands together. Write down each round. Count your chana at the end.

ask.q: Which choice earned you the most in a single round?
good: Cheating, when my partner played fair. I paid nothing and took 3.

flow.context: This is the second step of Pay or Cheat? Here you play Game 1, in which nobody can answer a cheat.

flow.do: 1. Start again with 10 chana each. 2. Play Game 2 for 8 rounds, with the 'No visit' rule. 3. Count the chana and add the two totals.
flow.say: Now we have a new rule. If I cheated last time, you may refuse to visit me this time.
flow.kid: Start again with 10 chana each. Play 8 rounds. If your partner cheated last round, you may say 'No visit'.
flow.context: This is the third step of Pay or Cheat? Here you play Game 2, in which a partner can refuse a cheater.

flow.do: 1. Compare the two games on the score sheet. 2. Count how many times each player cheated in each game. 3. Talk about what changed.
flow.say: In which game did we cheat more? In which game did the two of us together make more chana? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Compare the two games. In which game was there more cheating? In which game did you two make more together?

ask.q: What stops a real flower or a real bee from cheating all the time?
good: The partner can stop coming back. Bees learn which flowers are empty.
A cheater gains once, but loses the partner.

flow.parent: Most pairs cheat less in Game 2, but not all. Whatever happens, use your own results. In nature, bees learn to avoid flowers that pay nothing. Plants send less sugar to root fungi that give few minerals.

check.q: Both players play fair for all 8 rounds. How many chana does each one gain?
check.why: In each round a fair player pays 1 and takes 3, so they gain 2. Over 8 rounds that is 8 × 2 = 16. If you chose 24, you counted the 3 taken and forgot the 1 paid. Every trade has a cost.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pay or Cheat? Here you compare the two games and work out what keeps a trade fair.

experiments.title: The Crowded Cup Test: does a seedling grow better with 3 neighbours or with 63?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sow 4, 16 and 64 methi seeds in three cups of the same soil. Each cup gets the same water and the same light. After 14 days you compare the seedlings from each cup. You will find out whether a seedling grows better with a few neighbours or with many.
experiments.question: Three cups have the same soil, water and light. One holds 4 methi seedlings, one holds 16 and one holds 64. In which cup does each seedling grow best?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a seedling grow best with 3 neighbours, with 15 or with 63? Or will it make no difference? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: All three cups are the same size and hold soil from one mixed heap. They get the same number of spoons of water on the same days and stand side by side at one window. The seeds come from one packet. Only the number of seeds is different. You measure 4 seedlings from each cup, because one seedling can be unusual.
results_table: Soil before watering: wet, damp or dry

materials.item: paper or plastic cups of the same size, about as wide as your palm (cut-off bottle bottoms also work)
soil from a plant pot, or potting mix or cocopeat from a nursery, enough to fill the 3 cups
methi seeds from the kitchen (vendhayam), or mustard seeds if you have no methi
a tablespoon and a tumbler of water
a ruler with millimetre marks
a plate or tray to stand the cups on
a pen for marking the cups, a notebook and a sheet of white paper

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes in the cups with a nail or a compass point.

schedule.what: Fill the three cups, guess, and sow 4, 16 and 64 seeds. After this, give each cup 2 tablespoons of water every second day.
Count how many seedlings have come up in each cup.
Feel the soil in each cup before watering. Look at the cups from the side and write what you see.
Measure 4 seedlings from each cup, compare them side by side and explain the result.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw one seedling from each cup at the same scale, or take a photo of the three groups side by side. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.caption: 2. Give every cup the same water on the same days.

setup.caption: 3. On day 14, measure 4 seedlings from the middle of each cup.
