flow.do: 1. A grown-up makes 3 small holes in the bottom of each cup. 2. Tip all the soil into one heap and mix it with your hands. 3. Fill each cup to one finger-width below the rim. 4. Mark the cups A, B and C. 5. Pour 4 tablespoons of water into each cup and let it soak in.
flow.say: We mix the soil in one heap first, so that every cup gets the same soil. Why does that matter for our test?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to make holes in the cups. Mix all the soil in one heap. Fill the three cups the same. Mark them A, B and C. Give each cup 4 spoons of water.
flow.parent: The holes let extra water drain, so that no cup becomes waterlogged. Stand the cups on a plate.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Crowded Cup Test. Here you get three cups of the same soil ready.

flow.do: 1. Count out 4 seeds, 16 seeds and 64 seeds into three heaps. 2. Explain that each heap will share one cup. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Each cup has the same soil, water and light. In which cup will each seedling grow best?
flow.kid: Count 4 seeds, 16 seeds and 64 seeds. Each heap will share one cup. In which cup will a seedling grow best? Write your guess and your reason.

good: The cup with 4, because each one gets more water and room.
The cup with 64, because they can hold each other up. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
No difference, because the cups are the same. (A fair guess. The test will show.)

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This step of the Crowded Cup Test is for guessing. You guess in which cup a seedling will grow best, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Spread 4 seeds evenly on the soil of cup A. 2. Spread 16 seeds on cup B and 64 seeds on cup C. 3. Cover the seeds in each cup with a thin layer of soil, as thick as a coin. 4. Sprinkle 1 tablespoon of water on each. 5. Stand the cups side by side at a bright window.
flow.say: Spread the seeds out so that none are touching. From now on, every cup gets 2 tablespoons of water every second day.
flow.kid: Spread 4 seeds in cup A. Spread 16 in cup B and 64 in cup C. Cover them thinly with soil. Give each cup 1 spoon of water. Put the cups at a bright window.
flow.parent: Turn the tray round every two days, so that no cup is always nearest the glass. Keep to the same water for each cup, even when cup C looks thirsty. The shared water is part of the test.
flow.context: This is the sowing step of the Crowded Cup Test. Here you sow 4, 16 and 64 seeds and set the cups at a window.

flow.do: 1. Count the seedlings that have come up in each cup. 2. Write the three numbers in the table. 3. Water each cup with 2 tablespoons as usual.
flow.say: How many have come up in each cup? Do the seedlings in the three cups look different yet?
flow.kid: Count the seedlings in each cup. Write the numbers in your table. Do the cups look different yet?
flow.parent: In the first week the cups usually look alike, apart from the numbers. Each seedling is still living on the food stored in the seed.
flow.context: This is the day 4 check of the Crowded Cup Test. Here you count how many seeds have come up in each cup.

flow.do: 1. Before watering, push a finger into the soil of each cup. 2. Write wet, damp or dry for each cup. 3. Look at the cups from the side and compare the stems. 4. Water each cup with 2 tablespoons.
flow.say: Feel the soil in each cup before we water. Is it wet, damp or dry?
flow.kid: Push a finger into the soil of each cup. Which is the driest? Look from the side. Which stems are thinnest? Write what you see.

ask.q: All three cups got the same water. Why is one drier?
good: More seedlings drank the water.
Sixty-four roots take up more than four roots.

flow.parent: Cup C is usually the driest, because 64 seedlings draw up far more water than 4. If cup C wilts badly, write that down. Then give all three cups one extra watering of the same size.
flow.context: This is the day 8 check of the Crowded Cup Test. Here you find out which cup has used up the most water.

flow.do: 1. Count the seedlings that are leaning or fallen in each cup. 2. Choose 4 seedlings from the middle of cup B and cup C, and all 4 in cup A. 3. Measure each one from the soil to the top, in centimetres. 4. Measure the longest leaf on each one, in millimetres. 5. Loosen the soil with a spoon and lift those 12 seedlings out. 6. Rinse the roots and lay the seedlings on white paper in three groups.
flow.say: We take seedlings from the middle of the crowded cups. The ones at the edge get extra light from the side, so they are not typical.
flow.kid: Count the fallen seedlings in each cup. Measure 4 seedlings from the middle of each cup. Measure the height and the longest leaf. Lift them out and lay them on paper.

ask.q: Compare the three groups. What is different about the stems, the leaves and the roots?
good: The crowded ones are thinner and their leaves are smaller.
The crowded ones are as tall or taller, but they lean.
The ones with room have thicker stems and longer roots.

flow.parent: The usual result is that seedlings in cup C have the thinnest stems and smallest leaves, and more of them lean. They are often as tall as the others, or taller. If the three cups still look alike, keep them going and measure again on day 21. The differences grow with time.
flow.context: This is the measuring step of the Crowded Cup Test. Here you measure and compare 4 seedlings from each cup.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they found, and what in the table shows it. 2. Ask why they think it happened. 3. Only then read the explanation below together. 4. Your child writes the three sentences.
flow.say: What did you find? What in your table shows it? Why do you think it happened? Now let us read what scientists say and see if it matches.
flow.kid: Say what you found. Point to the numbers that show it. Say why you think it happened. Then write your three sentences.

ask.q: Did any seedling attack another seedling?
good: No. Each one just used water and light that the others needed.

ask.q: What could two methi seedlings give each other?
good: Nothing much. They both need the same things and make the same things.

flow.parent: The explanation: all the seedlings in a cup need the same water, minerals and light. With 64 sharing, each gets less. This is competition. Crowded seedlings also sense their neighbours through the light and grow longer, thinner stems. Plant the leftover seedlings in a bigger pot, or eat them as methi greens.

check.q: Sixty-four seedlings in one cup had thin stems and small leaves. What is the best explanation?
options: Each got a smaller share of water and light
check.why: All 64 seedlings needed the same water, minerals and light, so each got a small share. Nobody fought. If you chose 'fought', remember that competition only means using up what a neighbour also needs.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Crowded Cup Test. Here you say what you found and why, and then compare with what scientists say.

experiments.title: Lichen from the Spice Box: which takes up water faster, a dry lichen or a dry leaf?
experiments.context: In this experiment you use kalpasi, a dried lichen sold as a spice, and dried bay leaves. You put the same weight of each in water for 10 minutes and weigh them again. This shows how a lichen, who has no roots, gets water.
experiments.question: A dry lichen and a dry leaf of the same weight sit in water for 10 minutes. Which one takes up more water?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which will take up more water in 10 minutes: the dry lichen, the dry bay leaves, or both the same? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Both start dry and at the same weight. Both sit in the same amount of water, for the same 10 minutes, held under by a spoon. Both are shaken and dabbed in the same way before weighing. Only the kind of living being is different.

materials.item: kalpasi (also sold as dagad phool or black stone flower) from the spice shelf of a grocery shop
dried bay leaves (tej patta or biryani leaf), about 12
a kitchen weighing scale that shows grams
steel bowls of the same size, half full of water
spoons to hold the pieces under water
a clean cotton cloth, a clock and a notebook
a hand lens, or a phone camera for zooming in

schedule.what: Look at the dry lichen, guess, soak the lichen and the bay leaves for 10 minutes, weigh them again and explain the result.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the lichen from the top and from underneath, or take two photos. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: weight before and after 10 minutes in water
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child looking through a hand lens at a piece of grey-green kalpasi held between two fingers, showing the pale top and the black underside.
setup.caption: 1. Look at both sides of the dry lichen with a lens.

setup.art: A kitchen scale showing 5 grams with a heap of kalpasi on it, and a second heap of bay leaves waiting beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Weigh out the same weight of lichen and of bay leaves.

setup.art: Two steel bowls of water, one with kalpasi and one with bay leaves, each held under by a spoon, with a clock beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Hold both under water for 10 minutes.

setup.art: Wet kalpasi being dabbed on a cotton cloth, with the scale ready beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Shake, dab and weigh again.

flow.do: 1. Give your child one piece of dry kalpasi. 2. Look at the top side and the underside with the lens. 3. Bend a small piece and see what happens. 4. Ask what they notice and what they wonder.
flow.say: This is kalpasi, a spice. Kalpasi grows on trees and rocks. Look at both sides. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Look at both sides of the kalpasi with a lens. Bend a small piece. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

ask.q: Is this a leaf, a flower, a mushroom, or something else?
good: It has no stalk, no veins and no roots.
The top is pale and the underside is black.

flow.parent: Kalpasi is a dried leafy lichen. The top is grey or grey-green. The underside is black, often with tiny dark threads that held the bark. A dry piece crumbles when bent. Do not explain yet what a lichen is.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lichen from the Spice Box. Here you look closely at a dried lichen before the test.

flow.do: 1. Show the bay leaves next to the kalpasi. 2. Explain that both will sit in water for 10 minutes. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Both of these are dry. Both will sit in water for 10 minutes. Which will take up more water?
flow.kid: The lichen and the leaves will sit in water for 10 minutes. Which will take up more water? Write your guess and your reason.

good: The leaves, because leaves are from plants and plants need water. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
The lichen, because the lichen looks like a sponge.
The same, because both are dry. (A fair guess. The test will show.)

flow.context: This step of Lichen from the Spice Box is for guessing. You guess which will take up more water, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Put kalpasi on the scale until it shows 5 grams. 2. Weigh out 5 grams of bay leaves. 3. Write both dry weights in the table. 4. Put each into a bowl of water at the same moment. 5. Rest a spoon on top to hold the pieces under.
flow.say: We start with the same weight of each, so that the test is fair. Note the time now.
flow.kid: Weigh 5 grams of lichen. Weigh 5 grams of bay leaves. Write the weights down. Put each in a bowl of water. Hold them under with a spoon.
flow.parent: Kalpasi is very light, so 5 grams is a big handful. If your scale shows only whole grams, that is fine. With no scale, skip the weighing and compare by touch in the last steps.
flow.context: This is the weighing step of Lichen from the Spice Box. Here you weigh equal amounts of lichen and bay leaf and put them in water.

flow.do: 1. Wait 10 minutes. 2. While you wait, your child feels the top and the underside of a dry piece of kalpasi and says how they differ. 3. Now and then, look at the lichen in the water and note any change.
flow.say: While we wait, feel both sides of a dry piece. Is the top the same as the underside? Then watch the piece in the water.
flow.kid: Wait 10 minutes. Feel both sides of a dry piece and tell your grown-up how they differ. Watch the lichen in the water. Is anything changing?
flow.parent: The lichen usually goes soft and limp within a minute or two. The colour may change a little. Write down what you really see.
flow.context: This is the waiting step of Lichen from the Spice Box. Here you draw the lichen while both samples soak for 10 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Lift out the lichen and shake the pieces 10 times over the bowl. 2. Dab them once on the cloth and weigh them. 3. Do exactly the same with the bay leaves. 4. Write both wet weights. 5. Bend a piece of each.
flow.say: Shake and dab both in the same way. We want to weigh the water inside them, not the drops outside.
flow.kid: Lift out the lichen. Shake the pieces 10 times and dab them once. Weigh them. Do the same with the bay leaves. Write both weights. Bend a piece of each.
flow.parent: The usual result is that the lichen weighs two or three times as much as before and bends like wet cloth. The bay leaves gain much less and stay stiff.
flow.context: This is the second weighing step of Lichen from the Spice Box. Here you weigh the lichen and the bay leaves after 10 minutes in water.

flow.do: 1. Work out the water taken up by each: wet weight minus dry weight. 2. Ask what your child found and why they think it happened. 3. Then read the explanation together. 4. Your child writes the three sentences.
flow.say: What did you find? Why do you think one took up so much more? Now let us read what scientists say.
flow.kid: Work out the water each one took up. Say what you found. Say why you think it happened. Write your three sentences.

ask.q: A leaf on a tree gets water from the roots. Where does a lichen on a rock get water?
good: From rain and mist, straight through the surface.
A lichen has no roots.

flow.parent: The explanation: a leaf has a thin waxy skin that keeps water in, so it also keeps water out. A leaf gets water through the plant's roots and stem. A lichen has no roots and no waxy skin. The fungus threads soak up water over the whole surface, like a cloth. A lichen dries out between showers and starts working again when wet. Dry the kalpasi and bay leaves in the sun and cook with them this week.

check.q: Why can a dry lichen take up water so much faster than a dry leaf?
options: The lichen has no waxy skin
check.why: A lichen has no waxy skin, so water passes in over the whole surface. A leaf's waxy skin slows water down in both directions. If you chose 'long roots', remember that a lichen has no roots at all.

flow.context: This is the last step of Lichen from the Spice Box. Here you work out how much water each took up and explain the difference.

activities.title: The Trade Table: what does each partner give?
activities.context: In this activity you fill in a table of five partnerships. For each partner you write what they give and what they cannot make for themselves. Then you look for a pattern.

materials.item: a sheet of paper, a ruler and a pencil

activities.record: Keep the finished table. Under it, write one sentence about what all five partnerships have in common.

setup.art: A hand-drawn table with five rows named flower and bee, root and fungus, lichen, coral and alga, tur dal and bacteria, and four empty columns.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with five rows and four columns.

setup.art: A child writing 'sugar' in one box of the table and 'carries pollen' in the next.
setup.caption: 2. For each partner, write what they give.

setup.art: The finished table with a circle drawn around the column 'cannot make for themselves'.
setup.caption: 3. Look down the last columns. What do you notice?

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with 5 rows. 2. Name the rows: flower and bee, root and fungus, alga and fungus in a lichen, coral and alga, tur dal plant and root bacteria. 3. Make four columns: partner 1 gives, partner 2 gives, partner 1 cannot do, partner 2 cannot do.
flow.say: Here are five pairs of living beings who live better together. For each pair we will ask what each one gives.
flow.kid: Draw a table with 5 rows and 4 columns. Write the five pairs down the side. Write the four headings across the top.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Trade Table. Here you draw a table for five partnerships.

flow.do: 1. Read the facts in the note below aloud, one pair at a time. 2. After each pair, your child fills in that row. 3. Ask each time why that partner cannot do the other's job.
flow.say: Listen to the facts about this pair. What does each one give? What can each one not do alone?
flow.kid: Listen to the facts about each pair. Write what each partner gives. Write what each partner cannot do alone.
flow.parent: The facts. Flower: makes sugar, cannot move. Bee: flies between flowers, cannot make sugar. Root: gets sugar from the leaves, cannot reach far or into tiny gaps. Fungus: has very fine threads that reach far, cannot make sugar. Alga: makes sugar, dries out fast alone. Lichen fungus: holds water and grips rock, cannot make sugar. Alga in a coral: makes sugar, has no shelter alone. Coral animal: builds a hard home, cannot make sugar. Tur dal plant: makes sugar, cannot use the nitrogen in air. Root bacteria: can use the nitrogen in air, need sugar.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Trade Table. Here you fill in what each partner gives and what each cannot do.

flow.do: 1. Look down the columns together. 2. Ask what the five pairs have in common. 3. Ask whether two bees, or two flowers, could trade in this way.
flow.say: Look at all five rows. Could two bees be partners like this? Why, or why not?
flow.kid: Look at all five rows. Could two bees trade like this? Say why.

ask.q: What is the same about every pair?
good: One of them makes sugar and the other cannot.
The two are very different kinds of living beings.
Each gives what the other cannot make.

flow.parent: Let your child find the pattern. In every row, one partner makes sugar from sunlight and the other cannot. The two are always very different beings. Two bees have nothing to exchange, because they make and need the same things.

check.q: What is true of all five partnerships in the table?
options: The partners are the same size
Each gives what the other cannot easily get
check.why: In each pair, one partner makes something or does something the other cannot. If you chose 'both make sugar', look at the table again. In every row only one partner makes sugar.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Trade Table. Here you look for what all five partnerships have in common.

activities.title: Inside a Lichen: draw the four layers
activities.context: In this activity you draw a model of a leafy lichen cut through from top to bottom. A model is a drawing that explains what you cannot see. You will find out where the two partners live inside one body. You show where the fungus is, where the alga is, and what passes between them.

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper, a pencil and a green colour pencil or crayon
a piece of kalpasi, if you have some

activities.record: Keep your labelled drawing. Add arrows for water, sugar and light.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a long box divided into four bands from top to bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a tall box and divide it into four bands.

setup.art: The same box with the top band filled with tightly packed threads and the second band with green circles wrapped in threads.
setup.caption: 2. Draw packed threads on top, then green algal cells wrapped in threads.

setup.art: The finished drawing with labels and three arrows: light coming from above, water soaking in, sugar passing from a green cell to a thread.
setup.caption: 3. Label the layers and add arrows for light, water and sugar.

flow.do: 1. If you have kalpasi, tear a piece and look at the torn edge. 2. Ask your child to say where they think the fungus and the alga are inside a lichen. 3. Do not correct this first idea.
flow.say: A lichen is a fungus and an alga living as one body. Where do you think each one is? Tell me your idea first.
flow.kid: A lichen is a fungus and an alga in one body. Where is each one? Tell your grown-up what you think is inside.
flow.parent: Many children draw the fungus on one side and the alga on the other. Keep this first drawing to compare later.
flow.context: This is the first step of Inside a Lichen. Here you draw your own idea of where the two partners are.

flow.do: 1. Draw a tall box with four bands, or lay four strips of torn paper one above the other. 2. Top band: tightly packed fungus threads. 3. Second band: small green circles, each wrapped in threads. 4. Third band: loose threads with gaps of air. 5. Bottom band: packed threads again, with short threads hanging down to grip the bark.
flow.say: Scientists who cut a leafy lichen see four layers. The algae live in one thin band near the top.
flow.kid: Draw a tall box with four bands, or lay four paper strips. Show packed threads on top. Draw green cells wrapped in threads next. Draw loose threads, then packed threads with grips.

ask.q: Why do the algae live near the top and not at the bottom?
good: They need light to make sugar.
The skin above them lets some light through but stops them drying.

flow.context: This is the drawing step of Inside a Lichen. Here you draw the four layers that scientists see with a microscope.

flow.do: 1. Label the fungus and the alga. 2. Add an arrow for light from above. 3. Add arrows for water soaking in from the surface. 4. Add an arrow for sugar from a green cell to a thread. 5. Compare with the first drawing.
flow.say: Now add arrows. Where does the light come in? Where does the water come in? Where does the sugar go?
flow.kid: Label the fungus and the alga. Add arrows for light, water and sugar. Compare with your first drawing. What did you change?

check.q: In a lichen, which partner makes the sugar?
options: Neither: sugar comes from the bark
check.why: The alga is green and makes sugar from light, air and water. The fungus cannot make sugar. If you chose 'the bark', remember that lichens also grow on bare rock and glass, which give no food.

flow.context: This is the last step of Inside a Lichen. Here you label your model and show what passes between the partners.

activities.title: Lichen Walk: what do the tree trunks say about the air? (if you have trees or old walls nearby)
activities.context: In this activity you look for lichens on tree trunks in two places, one near a busy road and one in a quiet place. Lichens soak up whatever is in the rain and the air, so the kinds you find tell you about the air.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a hand lens or a phone camera

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along. Stay on the footpath and away from traffic.
activities.record: For each place, write how many trunks out of 5 had crusty, leafy or bushy lichens. Write one sentence comparing the two places.

setup.art: Three small drawings side by side: a flat crust painted onto bark, a leafy lichen with lifted edges, and a bushy lichen hanging like a small beard.
setup.caption: 1. Learn the three shapes: crusty, leafy and bushy.

setup.art: A child and a parent looking at a rain tree trunk at chest height beside a city road, the child pointing at a grey-green patch.
setup.caption: 2. Check 5 trunks in each place, at the height of your chest.

setup.art: A notebook page with a tally table for two places and three lichen shapes.
setup.caption: 3. Tally what you find and compare the two places.

flow.do: 1. Name the three lichen shapes aloud. 2. Crusty lichens lie flat, like paint. 3. Leafy lichens have edges you can lift. 4. Bushy lichens stand up or hang down like tiny shrubs. 5. Choose two places: one beside a busy road, one in a park or a quiet lane.
flow.say: Lichens come in three main shapes. Bushy ones are harmed most easily by dirty air. Crusty ones cope best. What might we find by the main road?
flow.kid: Say the three shapes: crusty, leafy and bushy. Which one lies flat like paint? Choose a busy road and a quiet place. What do you think you will find in each?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lichen Walk. Here you learn three lichen shapes and choose two places to compare.

flow.do: 1. In each place, choose 5 large trees or old walls. 2. Look at each one at chest height, all the way round. 3. Tick which shapes you find. 4. Look at one patch with the lens. 5. Do not pull any lichen off.
flow.say: Look all the way round the trunk. Is there any lichen? Which shape? Leave them where they are. They grow very slowly.
flow.kid: Go with a grown-up. Check 5 trunks in each place. Look all the way round. Tick the shapes you find. Do not pull any lichen off.
flow.parent: Green powder or a green film is alga living alone, not lichen. Moss is soft with tiny leaves. Lichen is usually grey, grey-green, yellow or orange and dry to the touch. In the middle of a big city you may find only crusts, or none at all. That is a real result. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Lichen Walk. Here you check five trunks in each of two places for lichens.

flow.do: 1. Count the trunks with lichen in each place. 2. Count how many shapes each place had. 3. Ask what could explain the difference, apart from the air.
flow.say: Which place had more lichen, and more shapes? Could anything besides the air explain it?
flow.kid: Count the trunks with lichen in each place. Which place had more shapes? What else could explain it, besides the air?

ask.q: What else, besides dirty air, could make one place have fewer lichens?
good: The trees are younger, and lichens grow slowly.
It is drier or sunnier there.
The bark is a different kind, or it has been painted.

flow.parent: Scientists use lichens to map air quality, but they compare many trees of the same kind and age. Your count is a first look, not a proof.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Lichen Walk. Here you compare the two places and think about what else could explain the result.

activities.title: Honest Visitor or Robber? Watch one flower for ten minutes (if you have flowers nearby)
activities.context: In this activity you watch the visitors to one kind of flower for ten minutes. For each visitor you note whether they went in at the front, past the pollen, or took nectar from the side.

materials.item: a plant with open flowers on a balcony, at a window or in a park (hibiscus, tulsi, tecoma, pumpkin and marigold all get visitors)
a notebook, a pencil and a clock

activities.safety: Watch from an arm's length away and do not touch the bees. They sting only when pressed or frightened.
activities.record: A tally of visitors in three columns: went in at the front, took nectar from the side, only sat on the flower. Add a photo or a drawing of the flower with the pollen marked.

setup.art: A child sitting an arm's length from a hibiscus bush on a balcony with a notebook on her knee.
setup.caption: 1. Sit an arm's length from the flowers and keep still.

setup.art: A close view of a flower with a bee entering at the open front and a second insect on the outside near the base.
setup.caption: 2. For each visitor, note where they went to feed.

setup.art: A notebook page with three tally columns and a small drawing of the flower.
setup.caption: 3. Tally the visitors and look for holes near the base of the flowers.

flow.do: 1. Look into one flower together. 2. Find the pollen, which is usually a yellow powder on small stalks. 3. Point to where the pollen is. 4. Ask where a visitor would have to go to reach the nectar.
flow.say: Where is the pollen on this flower? Nectar is usually at the bottom. Which way must a visitor go to reach it?
flow.kid: Look into one flower. Find the yellow pollen and point to it. Which way must a visitor go to reach the nectar?
flow.context: This is the first step of Honest Visitor or Robber? Here you find the pollen in a flower and draw it.

flow.do: 1. Sit still and watch the flowers for 10 minutes. 2. For each visitor, make a tally mark in one of three columns. 3. Front: went in past the pollen. 4. Side: fed through the side or base of the flower. 5. Sat: only rested.
flow.say: Each time someone visits, watch where they feed. Did they touch the pollen on the way?
flow.kid: Watch the flowers for 10 minutes. Make a tally mark for each visitor. Did they go in at the front, or feed from the side?
flow.parent: Morning is best, between 8 and 11. If nobody comes in 10 minutes, try another kind of flower or another time. Look near the base of long flowers for small slits or holes left by robbers.
flow.context: This is the watching step of Honest Visitor or Robber? Here you tally where each visitor feeds.

flow.do: 1. Add up each column. 2. Look for holes near the base of five flowers. 3. Ask who gained from each kind of visit.
flow.say: How many visitors touched the pollen? How many did not? Who gained from each kind of visit?
flow.kid: Add up each column. Look for small holes near the base of the flowers.

ask.q: A visitor who feeds from the side gets nectar. What does the plant get?
good: Nothing. The pollen was not touched, so none was carried.

check.q: A bee bites a hole near the base of a flower and drinks the nectar. Who gains?
options: Both the bee and the plant
check.why: The bee gets the nectar. The plant made the nectar and got no pollen carried, so the plant loses. If you chose 'both', check whether the bee touched the pollen.

flow.context: This is the last step of Honest Visitor or Robber? Here you count honest visits and robberies and say who gained.

activities.title: A Meal Without Partners: what would be left on my plate?
activities.context: In this activity you list everything in one meal and find the partnerships behind each food. Then you cross out every food that needed an animal pollinator, and see what is left.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
today's lunch or dinner, to look at

activities.record: A list of the foods in one meal, each marked P (needed or was helped by a pollinator), B (a pulse with root bacteria), M (made with microbes) or W (wind or no pollination).

setup.art: A steel plate with rice, sambar with pumpkin and drumstick, curd, a mango slice and a papad, seen from above.
setup.caption: 1. List every food in one meal, down to the spices.

setup.art: A notebook list of foods with the letters P, B, M and W written beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Mark each food with the partnership behind it.

setup.art: The same plate with the pumpkin, mango and mustard seeds faded out.
setup.caption: 3. Cross out the foods that needed a pollinator. What is left?

flow.do: 1. Choose one meal. 2. List every plant food in it, including oil and spices. 3. Count the foods.
flow.say: Let us list everything on this plate that came from a plant. Think of what is inside the sambar or the curry too.
flow.kid: Choose one meal. List every food in it that came from a plant. Do not forget the oil and the spices. Count them.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Meal Without Partners. Here you list every plant food in one meal.

flow.do: 1. Read the lists in the note below. 2. Mark each food P, B, M or W. 3. Count how many foods have each letter.
flow.say: Some foods form only after an animal carries pollen. Some are pulses with bacteria on their roots. Some are made by microbes. Let us mark each one.
flow.kid: Mark each food. P means a pollinator was needed. B means a pulse with root bacteria. M means made with microbes. W means wind or none.
flow.parent: P, needs an animal pollinator: pumpkin, all gourds, cucumber, watermelon, mango, cashew, cardamom, apple, almond. P, gives more with pollinators: mustard, coconut, coffee, sunflower, brinjal, tomato, chilli. B: every dal, chana, rajma, groundnut and beans. M: idli, dosa, curd, dhokla and bread. W, wind-pollinated or self-pollinated grains: rice, wheat, maize, ragi, jowar. W, grown from pieces of the plant: banana, potato, sugarcane. If a food is not listed, mark it with a question mark and look it up together.
flow.context: This is the main step of A Meal Without Partners. Here you mark each food with the partnership behind it.

flow.do: 1. Cross out every food marked P. 2. Look at what is left. 3. Ask what the meal would taste like, and what would be missing for health.
flow.say: Cross out everything that needed a pollinator. What is left on the plate? What has the meal lost?
flow.kid: Cross out every food marked P. What is left? What would this meal taste like now?

ask.q: The grains are still there. So why do pollinators matter for food?
good: Most fruits, many vegetables, oils and spices need them.
The meal would fill you, but it would lose much of its taste and vitamins.

flow.parent: Grains fill most of the plate and need no animal. But many fruits, vegetables, nuts and spices do. About 3 in 4 of the world's main crops give more with animal pollinators. Those crops make about a third of the world's food by weight.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Meal Without Partners. Here you cross out the foods that needed a pollinator and see what remains.

projects.title: Two Kinds in One Cup: do methi and mustard share better than methi and methi?
projects.context: This project follows the Crowded Cup Test, in which crowded methi seedlings grew thin. Here you ask a new question. Does a methi seedling grow better among 31 other methi, or among a mix of methi and mustard? Nobody can tell you the answer beforehand.

materials.item: cups of the same size, with holes, as in the Crowded Cup Test
soil from one mixed heap
methi seeds
mustard seeds
a tablespoon, a ruler and a notebook

projects.safety: A grown-up makes the holes in the cups with a nail or a compass point.

schedule.what: Sow three cups: 32 methi, 32 mustard, and 16 methi mixed with 16 mustard. Guess what will happen and why. Water each cup with 2 tablespoons every second day.
Count the seedlings of each kind in each cup. Note which kind is taller.
Measure 4 methi seedlings from the middle of the methi cup and 4 from the mixed cup. Do the same for mustard.
Measure again, lay the seedlings out side by side, and write a short report.

projects.record: A table for days 14 and 21: height and longest leaf for 4 methi seedlings and 4 mustard seedlings from each cup. Then a report of five sentences: question, guess, what you did, what you found, and one thing you would change next time.

setup.art: Three cups in a row labelled 'methi 32', 'mustard 32' and 'mixed 16 + 16', with two small heaps of different seeds beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Sow one cup of methi, one of mustard and one mixed.

setup.art: The three cups after two weeks, the mixed cup showing two kinds of seedlings with differently shaped leaves growing together.
setup.caption: 2. Give every cup the same water and light for 21 days.

setup.art: Four methi seedlings from the methi cup and four from the mixed cup laid side by side on white paper next to a ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Compare methi from the methi cup with methi from the mixed cup.

flow.do: 1. Prepare three cups of soil as in the Crowded Cup Test. 2. Sow 32 methi seeds in cup 1 and 32 mustard seeds in cup 2. 3. Mix 16 methi and 16 mustard and sow them in cup 3. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason. 5. Water all three the same.
flow.say: Every cup has 32 seeds. In the mixed cup, will the methi do better, worse or the same as in the methi cup? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sow 32 methi in cup 1. Sow 32 mustard in cup 2. Sow 16 of each in cup 3. Will methi grow better in cup 1 or cup 3? Write your guess and reason.
flow.parent: Both guesses are reasonable. If the two kinds use the soil and light a little differently, each may do better in the mix. If one kind grows faster and shades the other, the slower kind may do worse.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Kinds in One Cup. Here you sow three cups and guess how methi will do in a mixed cup.

flow.do: 1. Count the seedlings of each kind in each cup. 2. Note which kind came up first and which is taller. 3. Keep watering all cups the same.
flow.say: Which kind came up first? Which is taller now? What might that mean for the other kind?
flow.kid: Count the seedlings of each kind. Which kind is taller? Write it down. Keep watering all cups the same.
flow.context: This is the day 7 check of Two Kinds in One Cup. Here you count the seedlings and note which kind is ahead.

flow.do: 1. Measure the height and longest leaf of 4 methi seedlings from the middle of cup 1. 2. Do the same for 4 methi seedlings in cup 3. 3. Do the same for mustard in cups 2 and 3. 4. Do not pull any out yet.
flow.say: We compare methi with methi, and mustard with mustard.
flow.kid: Measure 4 methi seedlings in cup 1 and 4 in cup 3. Measure mustard in cups 2 and 3. Write the numbers. Do not pull them out.

ask.q: Why compare methi only with methi?
good: The two kinds grow differently anyway.
We want to know what the neighbours changed, so only the neighbours should differ.

flow.context: This is the day 14 check of Two Kinds in One Cup. Here you measure each kind in the pure cup and in the mixed cup.

flow.do: 1. Measure the same things again. 2. Lift out 4 seedlings of each kind from each cup and lay them side by side. 3. Ask what your child found and why they think so. 4. Your child writes the report.
flow.say: Did methi do better among methi, or in the mix? What about mustard? What do you think happened under the soil and above it?
flow.kid: Measure again. Lay the seedlings side by side. Did methi grow better in the mix? Did mustard? Write your report.
flow.parent: There is no fixed right answer. Farmers and scientists get both results with different pairs of crops. In Karnataka, many farmers sow rows of pulses such as avarai and togari between rows of ragi. Those pairs usually do well together, partly because pulses get nitrogen through their root bacteria.

check.q: In a mixed cup, methi grew better than in a cup of only methi. What is the most likely reason?
options: The two kinds needed slightly different things
check.why: If two kinds use light, water or minerals a little differently, each leaves more for the other than a twin would. This is a game moment. Your own cups may have shown the opposite, and that is a real result too.

flow.context: This is the last step of Two Kinds in One Cup. Here you compare the seedlings and write a report.

challenges.title: A Flower That Cannot Be Robbed
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Some bees bite a hole in the side of a flower and take the nectar without touching the pollen. Here you design a paper flower that an honest visitor can use easily and a robber cannot.
challenges.problem: Build a paper flower with a chana at the bottom as the nectar and a ring of atta inside the mouth as the pollen. A finger entering at the mouth must reach the chana and come out with atta on it. A robber with a toothpick must not be able to touch the chana through the side within 10 seconds.
constraints: The honest finger must reach the nectar through the mouth in 5 seconds or less.
Use only paper, tape, cloth, leaves and string.
The flower must stay open at the mouth. No lids.
materials: 4 sheets of paper, and old newspaper
a teaspoon of atta or haldi
a toothpick or a sharp pencil for the robber
general: Make the wall at the base thicker, with several layers of paper. Many real flowers have a tough green cup around the base.
Make the tube long and narrow, so that the nectar is far from the mouth and hard to find from outside.
Tape a second tube inside the first, so that the nectar does not touch the outer wall.
creative: Pack several flowers tightly side by side, as in a marigold head, so that their sides are covered by their neighbours.
Wrap the base in overlapping cloth or leaf pieces, like the leafy cups under some flowers.
Hang the flower mouth-down on a string, so that a robber has nowhere to stand and bite.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own flower. Draw it or describe it, build it and test it 3 times with a robber and 3 times with an honest finger. What did your design cost in extra paper? A real flower pays for thick walls with food she could have used to make seeds.

setup.art: A simple paper tube taped shut at the bottom, standing on a table, with a chana inside at the base and a ring of white atta just inside the open mouth.
setup.caption: 1. Build a plain paper flower with a chana at the bottom and atta at the mouth.

setup.art: One child poking a toothpick through the side of the paper tube near the base while another child times with a clock.
setup.caption: 2. Let a robber try to touch the chana through the side in 10 seconds.

setup.art: A redesigned paper flower with a thick layered base and a narrow tube, and a finger coming out of its mouth dusted with atta.
setup.caption: 3. Redesign the flower, then test the robber and the honest finger again.

flow.do: 1. Roll a sheet of paper into a tube as long as your finger, and tape it. 2. Fold and tape one end shut. 3. Drop in a chana. 4. Dab a ring of atta just inside the mouth. 5. One player is the robber with a toothpick, and has 10 seconds.
flow.say: This plain flower pays every visitor. Let us see how long a robber needs to reach the nectar through the side.
flow.kid: Roll a paper tube and tape one end shut. Drop in a chana. Dab atta inside the mouth. Now let a robber try with a toothpick for 10 seconds.
flow.parent: The robber will reach the chana in a second or two. That is the problem to solve.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Flower That Cannot Be Robbed. Here you build a plain paper flower and see how easily it is robbed.

flow.do: 1. Ask for three ideas to stop the robber, drawn or told. 2. Read the usual and the creative solutions together. 3. Your child chooses one design and builds it. 4. Check that a finger can still reach the chana through the mouth.
flow.say: How could a flower keep robbers out and still let honest visitors in? Draw or tell three ideas. Which one will you build, and why?
flow.kid: Draw or tell three ideas to stop the robber. Choose one and build it. Check that your finger can still reach the chana through the mouth.
flow.context: This is the design step of A Flower That Cannot Be Robbed. Here you draw ideas, choose one and build it.

flow.do: 1. Test the robber 3 times, for 10 seconds each. 2. Test the honest finger 3 times, and check for atta on the finger each time. 3. Count the sheets of paper used. 4. Talk about the cost.
flow.say: Did the robber get in? Did the honest finger come out with pollen? How much more paper did this flower need than the first one?
flow.kid: Test the robber 3 times. Test the honest finger 3 times. Did the finger come out with atta? Count the paper you used.

ask.q: Thick walls stop robbers. Why don't all flowers have very thick walls?
good: Thick walls cost the plant food and water.
If robbers are rare, the cost is not worth it.

flow.context: This is the testing step of A Flower That Cannot Be Robbed. Here you test your design against a robber and an honest visitor.

items.p: Two kinds of living beings live together and both gain. What is this called?
items.why: In mutualism both partners gain more than they lose. In competition both lose, and in parasitism one loses.

items.p: True or false: in science, the word symbiosis always means that both partners are helped.
items.why: False. Symbiosis only means two kinds living closely together. It can help both, help one, or harm one. A strong answer gives an example of each.

items.p: When living beings need the same scarce resource, they are in ____ with each other.
a: competition
items.why: Competition needs no fighting. Each one simply uses up some of what the others need.

items.p: Sort these pairs by what happens to the two beings.
items.a: see items
items.why: Partners who both gain are very different beings who exchange something. Those who both lose need the same things. In the last group one feeds on the other.
items: a bee and a pumpkin flower
Both gain
two tomato plants in one small pot
Both lose
a mosquito and a person
One gains, one loses
a root fungus and a mango tree
Both gain
weeds and paddy in one field
Both lose
a louse and a child
One gains, one loses

items.p: Match each partner to what they give.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: In every partnership, each side gives something the other cannot easily make or do.

items.p: In the Crowded Cup Test, which cup had the thinnest seedlings? Explain why, using the word 'share'.
items.a: The cup with 64 seeds. All 64 seedlings had to share the same water, minerals and light as the 4 seedlings in the first cup, so each one got much less.
items.why: A strong answer uses a result from the child's own table. It says that the seedlings needed the same things, so more seedlings meant a smaller share for each.

items.p: What do seedlings in a crowded cup compete for?
items.why: Seedlings need water and minerals from the soil and light from above. Nectar and pollen belong to flowers and their visitors.

items.p: Draw a lichen cut through from top to bottom. Show where the fungus is and where the alga is.
items.a: A drawing with fungus threads at the top and bottom, and a thin band of green algal cells just under the top skin, each wrapped in threads.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the algae near the top, where the light is, and shows that the fungus makes most of the body.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: In three of these pairs both partners gain. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A louse gains and the child loses, which is parasitism. In the other three pairs, both sides gain.

items.p: True or false: a lichen takes in water through roots.
items.why: False. A lichen has no roots. Water soaks in over the whole surface from rain and mist. The small threads underneath only grip the bark or rock.

items.p: A bee visits two pumpkin flowers. Put what happens in order.
a: The bee lands on the first flower to drink nectar
Pollen sticks to her hairy body
She flies to a second flower
Some pollen rubs off inside the second flower
A small pumpkin begins to grow
items.why: The bee comes for food. Carrying pollen is what the plant gets from the visit, and a fruit can grow only after pollen arrives.
items: She flies to a second flower
A small pumpkin begins to grow
The bee lands on the first flower to drink nectar
Some pollen rubs off inside the second flower
Pollen sticks to her hairy body

items.p: A partnership between a fungus and the roots of a plant is called a ____.
a: mycorrhiza
items.why: The word means 'fungus-root'. More than 8 of every 10 kinds of land plants have one.

items.p: A farmer's seedlings have come up very thickly in her nursery bed. Two neighbours give her advice.
items.a: A strong answer uses the Crowded Cup Test: crowded seedlings share water and light, so they grow thin and fall easily. It also sees the other side: pulling seedlings wastes seed and work, and some seedlings will die anyway, so a few spare ones are useful.
items.why: Both neighbours want a good crop. Thinning gives each plant more, and keeping spares guards against losses. Real farmers do some of both.

views.says: Pull out half of them now. The ones left will have room and grow strong.
Leave them all. More seedlings means more plants, and some always die.

items.ask: Which neighbour do you agree with? Use what you saw in the Crowded Cup Test. Then say one thing the other neighbour has right.

items.p: A bee and a flower can be partners. Two bees at one small flower compete. Why?
opts: The bee and the flower need different things
items.why: The flower needs pollen carried and the bee needs sugar, so they can exchange. Two bees both need the same nectar, so each leaves less for the other.

items.p: Kalpasi is sold as 'stone flower'. Explain why kalpasi is not a flower.
items.a: Kalpasi is a lichen, which is a fungus and an alga living as one body. A flower is a part of a plant that makes seeds. A lichen has no flowers, seeds, roots or leaves.
items.why: A strong answer says what a lichen is and names at least one thing a flower has that a lichen lacks.

items.p: A plant makes sugar easily. Why does a plant need a fungus to get phosphate from the soil?
items.a: Phosphate sticks to soil grains and hardly moves, so a root soon uses up what is nearby. Fungal threads are far thinner than roots and spread much farther, so they reach phosphate the root cannot.
items.why: A strong answer gives both reasons: the mineral does not move to the root, and the threads are thin and far-reaching.

items.p: Scientists found that plants sent more sugar to fungi that gave more phosphate. What does this show?
opts: Phosphate is a kind of sugar
items.why: The plant gave more to the partner who gave more. This keeps the trade fair, because a fungus that gives little gets little.

items.p: True or false: a carpenter bee who bites a hole in the side of a flower is pollinating that flower.
items.why: False. She drinks through the hole and does not touch the pollen, so none is carried. This is nectar robbing.

items.p: Taking nectar through a hole in the flower, without touching the pollen, is called nectar ____.
a: robbing
items.why: The robber gets the payment without doing the work. The plant loses the nectar.

items.p: Sort each fact about a lichen: is it true of the fungus or of the alga?
items.a: see items
items.why: The alga is the food-maker and needs light. The fungus builds the body, holds the water and grips the surface.
items: makes sugar from sunlight
Alga
holds water like a cloth
Fungus
grips the rock or bark
Fungus
is green
Alga
makes most of the body
Fungus
lives in a thin layer near the top
Alga

items.p: In heavily fertilised soil, a plant with root fungi may grow a little less. Why?
opts: The plant pays sugar but needs little help
items.why: In rich soil the plant can get phosphate alone. The fungus still takes sugar, so the plant pays for something they hardly need.

items.p: Draw a root and a fungus under the ground. Add one arrow for sugar and one for minerals.
items.a: A root with fine threads spreading far into the soil. A sugar arrow goes from root to fungus. A minerals arrow goes from fungus to root.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the threads reaching farther than the root, and the two arrows pointing in opposite directions.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: Scientists disagree about the alga inside a lichen.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence. For partnership: the alga lives on bare rock and in harsh sun only inside a lichen. For farming: the fungus takes much of the sugar, and many of these algae live alone while the fungus cannot. A good test compares how well the alga grows and spreads inside and outside lichens.
items.why: This is a real disagreement. What matters is using evidence and saying what could be measured to settle it.

views.who: A scientist who calls a lichen a partnership
views.says: The alga gets a damp, shaded home. Inside a lichen, algae live on bare rock where they could never live alone.

views.who: A scientist who calls it farming
views.says: The fungus takes much of the alga's sugar, and the alga grows more slowly. Many of these algae can live alone, but the fungus cannot.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger? Give one piece of evidence. Then say what you would measure to test it.

items.p: Bare rock slowly becomes soil. Put the steps in order.
a: Lichens settle on the bare rock
The lichens hold water and slowly wear the rock
Dust and dead lichen pieces collect
Mosses grow in the thin layer
Small plants take root
items.why: Lichens need no soil, so they can come first. Each newcomer makes the place a little easier for the next.
items: Mosses grow in the thin layer
Lichens settle on the bare rock
Small plants take root
Dust and dead lichen pieces collect
The lichens hold water and slowly wear the rock

items.p: In Lichen from the Spice Box, the lichen took up far more water than the bay leaves. Explain why.
items.a: A leaf has a waxy skin that slows water going in or out. A lichen has no waxy skin and no roots, so the fungus threads soak up water over the whole surface.
items.why: A strong answer compares the two surfaces and links this to how a lichen gets water from rain and mist.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are the words needed to talk about partnerships. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: sweet liquid a flower makes for visitors
simple green being who makes food from sunlight
something a living being needs and uses up
takes from a partner and gives little back

items.p: Bushy lichens hang from trees in a hill town but not in a city centre. What is the most likely reason?
items.why: Lichens soak up whatever the rain and air carry, and bushy kinds are harmed most easily. A careful scientist would also check the age of the trees and how damp each place is.

items.p: Three of these plants need animals to carry their pollen. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Rice pollen falls within the same flower or is carried by wind. Pumpkin, mango and cardamom all need insects.

items.p: Draw a tube-shaped flower cut in half. Label the nectar, the pollen, and where a robber would bite.
a: Nectar: at the bottom of the tube
Pollen: near the mouth, where a visitor brushes past
Robber's hole: in the side wall near the base
items.why: The pollen sits on the honest path to the nectar. A robber's hole is a shortcut that misses the pollen.
items.art: A blank box for the child's own drawing of a flower cut in half.

items.p: Some flowers make no nectar and still get visited. Why can't every flower cheat like this?
items.a: Bees learn which flowers are empty and stop visiting them. Cheating works only when cheaters are few and look like the many flowers that do pay.
items.why: A strong answer says that visitors learn, so a trick works only while it is rare.

items.p: Marked carbon from one seedling turned up in a neighbouring seedling. Name two ways the carbon could have travelled.
items.a: It could have passed through fungal threads joining the two roots. It could also have leaked from one root into the soil and been taken up by the other root.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different paths. Good science asks what else could explain a result before accepting the most exciting answer.

items.p: Do big trees feed small trees through fungi? Scientists disagree.
items.a: A strong answer says exactly what would count as evidence. For example: block only the fungal threads with a fine mesh, leave the soil path open, and see whether the carbon still arrives and whether the seedlings grow less.
items.why: Both sides agree that fungi join roots and that some carbon moves. They disagree about how much, by which path, and whether it helps. A good test separates the paths.

views.says: Big trees pass carbon to shaded seedlings through shared fungi, and this helps the seedlings to live.
The amounts are small, and few tests were done in real forests. The carbon could have moved through the soil.

views.who: A scientist thinking about the fungus
views.says: Why would a fungus carry food between trees for nothing? The fungus may be moving food for their own use.

items.ask: Whose view do you find strongest? Describe one test that could change your mind.

items.p: You want to test whether a root fungus helps a plant. What should you compare?
opts: One kind of plant, with and without fungus
Plants in sun and plants in shade
items.why: Only the fungus should differ. Soil, water, light and the kind of plant must be the same, as the cups were in the Crowded Cup Test.

items.p: Orchid seeds sprout on old bark but not on clean bark. How could you check that a fungus is the reason?
items.a: Put seeds on clean bark with the fungus added and on clean bark without, and keep everything else the same. If only the seeds with the fungus grow, the fungus is the reason.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing and has a comparison. It may add that old bark also holds more water, so that must be kept the same.

items.p: True or false: the mitochondria in your cells have their own genes.
items.why: True. Their genes are separate from the genes in the rest of the cell, and are most like the genes of certain bacteria.

items.p: Which evidence best shows that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria?
opts: Their genes are like the genes of bacteria
items.why: Many things are small or use food. Genes that match those of bacteria point to a shared family history.

items.p: In Pay or Cheat?, cheating earns the most in one round. Why does it earn less over many rounds?
items.a: A partner who has been cheated can refuse to visit again. The cheater gains 3 once and then gets nothing, while two fair players each gain 2 in every round.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers from the game and says that the partner's answer to a cheat is what changes the result.

items.p: A living being whose presence tells us about the air or water of a place is called a ____.
a: bioindicator
items.why: Lichens are bioindicators of clean air, because they soak up what the rain carries.

items.p: Sort each statement: do most scientists agree, or do they still argue?
items.a: see items
items.why: Agreed statements have been tested many times in many places. The argued ones rest on few tests, or on tests that can be read in more than one way.
items: Most land plants have fungus partners on their roots
Most agree
Old trees feed young trees through fungi
Still argued
A lichen holds a fungus and a green partner
Most agree
The alga in a lichen gains as much as the fungus
Still argued
Crowded plants of one kind compete
Most agree
The yeast found in lichens is a third partner
Still argued

items.p: One-celled animals who eat the same food cannot share a tube for long. Why can one who eats different food stay?
opts: They do not compete for food
items.why: Competition comes from needing the same resource. A being who uses a different food leaves the others' food alone.

items.p: Put these partnerships in order, from the loosest to the closest.
a: A butterfly visiting a flower
A fungus joined to a tree root
A fungus and an alga in a lichen
Mitochondria inside a cell
items.why: The butterfly and flower meet for seconds. The root and fungus are joined but separate. The lichen partners share one body. Mitochondria can never leave the cell.
items: A fungus and an alga in a lichen
Mitochondria inside a cell
A butterfly visiting a flower
A fungus joined to a tree root

items.p: Some people say nature is only a fight. Give one piece of evidence for this and one against.
items.a: For: crowded seedlings each get less, and predators kill prey. Against: most plants depend on root fungi and pollinators, and lichens and our own cells are partnerships.
items.why: A strong answer treats both sides fairly and uses examples from the child's own tests or from this lesson.

items.p: Match each partnership to something that can break it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A partnership lasts only while both sides gain. Change the conditions and the trade can stop.
pairs: the seed lands where the fungus is absent

items.p: Three of these pairs would compete strongly. Which pair would not?
opts: Two methi seedlings in one cup
items.why: The fungus and the alga need different things and each makes what the other lacks. The other pairs need the same resource.

items.p: Draw a line from 'mutualism' to 'parasitism'. Mark where a root fungus sits in poor soil and in rich soil.
a: Poor soil: near the mutualism end
Rich, fertilised soil: nearer the parasitism end
items.why: In poor soil the plant gains a lot for the sugar paid. In rich soil the plant pays the same and gains little, so the partnership slides along the line.
items.art: A blank box for the child's own drawing of a line with two marks.

quiz.p: A cattle egret eats insects stirred up by a buffalo. The buffalo is not affected. What is this called?
quiz.why: One gains and the other is neither helped nor harmed. If you chose mutualism, ask what the buffalo gets. In this case, very little.

quiz.p: Why were the seedlings in the 64-seed cup thinner than those in the 4-seed cup?
opts: Each got less water and light
quiz.why: All the cups had the same water, soil and light. With 64 sharing, each seedling got less. Nobody attacks anybody in competition.

quiz.p: Why do we measure seedlings from the middle of a crowded cup, not the edge?
opts: Middle seedlings are easier to reach
Edge seedlings get extra light from the side
Edge seedlings are a different kind
quiz.why: A seedling at the edge has neighbours on only one side, so they are less crowded than the rest. Measuring them would hide the effect of crowding.

quiz.p: A flower gives nectar and a bee carries pollen. Why is this a good trade for both?
opts: Each gives what the other cannot do
quiz.why: A plant makes sugar easily but cannot move. A bee flies easily but cannot make sugar. Kindness is not needed for a trade to work.

quiz.p: What does a root fungus get from the plant?
quiz.why: A fungus cannot make sugar, so the plant's sugar is the payment. Phosphate goes the other way, from the fungus to the plant.

quiz.p: Why can fungal threads reach minerals that roots cannot?
opts: They are far thinner and spread farther
quiz.why: Hyphae are many times thinner than the finest root, so they enter tiny gaps and spread beyond the soil the root has used up.

quiz.p: True or false: a lichen is a kind of moss.
quiz.why: False. A moss is a small plant with tiny leaves. A lichen is a fungus and an alga living as one body, with no leaves at all.

quiz.p: Lichens are among the first living beings to be harmed by dirty air. Why?
opts: They soak up rain and dust all over
quiz.why: A lichen has no waxy skin and no roots. Whatever is in the rain and dust goes straight in.

quiz.p: An orchid makes no nectar but looks like a flower that does. A bee visits. Who gains?
quiz.why: The orchid gets pollen carried and pays nothing. The bee spends time and effort for no food. The orchid is a cheater.

quiz.p: The same fungus helps a plant in poor soil but not in rich soil. Why?
opts: The fungus dies in rich soil
In rich soil the plant needs little help
quiz.why: A trade is worth making only if you need what the other side offers. In rich soil the plant can get minerals alone, but still pays sugar.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: Whether a lichen holds a fungus
Whether old trees feed young trees through fungi
quiz.why: The first three have been tested many times. The idea that trees feed each other through fungi rests on few tests in real forests, and scientists read them differently.

applications: Farmers thin their seedlings and space their plants, so that each plant gets enough light, water and minerals.
Farmers in many parts of India grow pulses between rows of millets, because the two kinds share a field well and the pulses' root bacteria bring in nitrogen.
Root fungi and root bacteria are grown and sold to farmers as biofertilisers, to be mixed with seeds or soil.
Beekeepers place hive boxes in coconut, mustard, cardamom and apple farms, because more bee visits mean more fruit and seed.
Scientists map air quality by recording which lichens grow on tree trunks.
Lichens give us spices such as kalpasi, and the dye in litmus paper that shows acids and alkalis.
Orchid nurseries raise seedlings either with the right fungus or on a jelly that contains sugar, because an orchid seed has no food store.

open_questions.q: What does the yeast inside a lichen do?
open_questions.why_open: The yeast was found only in 2016. Scientists have not agreed on whether the lichen needs the yeast, or whether the yeast is a partner, a lodger or a parasite.

open_questions.q: How much food really moves between trees through shared fungi, and does it help them?
open_questions.why_open: It is very hard to follow carbon under a real forest without digging up what you are studying. The few tests can be read in more than one way.

open_questions.q: Why can so few lichens be grown from their separate partners in a laboratory?
open_questions.why_open: The fungus and the alga can often be grown apart, but getting them to build a lichen body together usually fails. Something about how they recognise and shape each other is still unknown.

open_questions.q: How do a root and a fungus measure what the other is giving?
open_questions.why_open: Tests show that each sends more to a better partner. How a root or a hypha, with no brain, keeps count is only partly understood.

open_questions.q: Can corals take up new algae that cope with warmer seas, fast enough to survive?

maths.problem: A cup's soil surface is about 48 square centimetres. How much surface does each seedling get when the cup holds 4, 16 and 64 seedlings?
maths.answer: 12 square centimetres, 3 square centimetres and 0.75 square centimetres.
maths.explain: Divide the surface by the number of seedlings. 48 ÷ 4 = 12. 48 ÷ 16 = 3. 48 ÷ 64 = 0.75. Each time the seedlings become 4 times as many, each one's share becomes a quarter of what it was.
maths.context: This is about the Crowded Cup Test. There you sow 4, 16 and 64 methi seeds in three cups of the same size.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows how small each seedling's share becomes. It turns 'crowded' into a number you can compare.

maths.problem: Here are made-up leaf lengths for 4 seedlings from each cup. Find the average for each cup. Which cup's average is lowest?
maths.answer: Cup A: 14 mm. Cup B: 12 mm. Cup C: 8 mm. Cup C is lowest.
maths.explain: Add the four lengths and divide by 4. Cup A: 15 + 13 + 14 + 14 = 56, and 56 ÷ 4 = 14. Cup B: 12 + 11 + 13 + 12 = 48, and 48 ÷ 4 = 12. Cup C: 8 + 9 + 7 + 8 = 32, and 32 ÷ 4 = 8.
maths.context: This is about the Crowded Cup Test. There you measure the longest leaf on 4 seedlings from each cup on day 14. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: length of the longest leaf (mm)

maths.why_maths: One seedling can be unusually big or small. An average of four gives a fairer picture of the whole cup.

maths.problem: The cups hold 4, 16 and 64 seeds. What comes next in the pattern? A methi seed lying flat covers about 0.12 square centimetres. Would that many seeds fit on 48 square centimetres?
maths.answer: 256 seeds. They would fit, but only just: they would cover about 31 of the 48 square centimetres.
maths.explain: Each number is 4 times the one before, so the next is 64 × 4 = 256. The seeds would cover 256 × 0.12 = 30.72 square centimetres, which is nearly two thirds of the surface. The seeds would almost touch before they had even sprouted.
maths.context: This is about the Crowded Cup Test. There you sow 4, 16 and 64 methi seeds on soil in three cups.
maths.why_maths: Following the pattern one step further shows where crowding reaches its limit, without having to sow the cup.

maths.problem: In a made-up result, 5 grams of dry lichen weighed 13 grams after soaking. 5 grams of bay leaves weighed 6 grams. How many times as much water did the lichen take up?
maths.explain: The lichen took up 13 − 5 = 8 grams of water. The bay leaves took up 6 − 5 = 1 gram. 8 ÷ 1 = 8. So the lichen took up 8 times as much water as the same weight of bay leaves.
maths.context: This is about Lichen from the Spice Box. There you soak the same weight of dried lichen and dried bay leaves for 10 minutes and weigh them again. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the water taken up, and not just the final weights, shows how different the two really are.

maths.problem: A round lichen patch on a wall is 9 centimetres wide. Suppose the patch grows 2 millimetres wider each year. About how old is the patch?
maths.explain: First change to the same unit: 9 centimetres is 90 millimetres. Then divide: 90 ÷ 2 = 45. So the patch took about 45 years to grow. Real lichens grow between about 1 and 5 millimetres a year, so this is only a rough age.
maths.context: This is about the Lichen Walk. There you look for lichen patches on tree trunks and old walls.
maths.why_maths: Nobody watched the lichen arrive. Dividing size by growth rate is how scientists estimate the age of a lichen, and of the wall under it.

maths.problem: In Pay or Cheat?, a bee cheats in every round. The flower plays fair for 2 rounds, then refuses all visits. How many chana does the bee gain in 8 rounds? Compare this with a bee who plays fair for 8 rounds with a fair flower.
maths.answer: The cheating bee gains 6. The fair bee gains 16.
maths.explain: The cheating bee pays nothing and takes 3 in each of the first 2 rounds: 2 × 3 = 6. After that there are no visits, so she gains nothing more. A fair bee pays 1 and takes 3 in every round, so she gains 2 each time: 8 × 2 = 16.
maths.context: This is about the game Pay or Cheat? There a flower and a bee each choose, round after round, to pay or to cheat.
maths.why_maths: Adding up over many rounds shows something one round hides: a cheater wins a round and loses the game.

how_we_found_out.context: This card tells how people found out that a lichen is more than one living being, and how the answer changed twice.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people who studied lichens thought each lichen was a single plant. They named thousands of kinds. In 1867 a Swiss botanist, Simon Schwendener, said something startling at a meeting of scientists. He had studied lichens through his microscope. Every lichen, he said, is a fungus with tiny green algae living inside. Most lichen experts rejected the idea. William Nylander, the best known of them, mocked it and never accepted it. James Crombie in Britain complained that it made the fungus a master and the alga a slave. But through the 1870s and 1880s other scientists tested the idea, and the evidence for two partners piled up. In the end it went into every textbook. Then, in 2016, Toby Spribille and his team read the genes inside lichens. They found a third being that microscopes had missed for 150 years: a yeast, living in the lichen's skin. The two-partner picture had been incomplete too.
how_we_found_out.who: Simon Schwendener, a Swiss botanist, and Toby Spribille with his team in 2016
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed that each lichen was one single plant. Schwendener showed with a microscope that a lichen is a fungus with algae inside, and other scientists confirmed it over the next twenty years. In 2016 a third partner, a yeast, was found in many lichens.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in 1860s clothes bent over a brass microscope with a lichen on the slide, and beside him a round view showing fungal threads wrapped around green cells.

roots.context: We have learned how living beings compete and how they trade as partners. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Crowded Cup Test, 64 methi seedlings needed the same light, water and minerals from one cup. They grew thinner than the seedlings with room. A fungus and a root need different things, and each can get what the other lacks. Every partnership in this lesson joins two beings who are very different in this way.
deep_truth.habit: We expect those who are alike to get along best, and those who are very different to have little to do with each other. Among living beings sharing one place, likeness means needing the same things. Difference means having something the other lacks.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Crowded Cup Test, the usual result is that seedlings of one kind grow thinner as their numbers rise. Use what you really saw. In the Trade Table, every pair of partners was made of two very different beings: a plant and an insect, a plant and a fungus, a fungus and an alga. In each pair, only one could make sugar.

three.who_am_i: Every cell of your body holds mitochondria, which were once free-living bacteria. Microbes in your gut digest part of your food. Your body is built from partnerships.
three.what_is_life: No kind of living being makes everything they need. Each one lives by exchanging with others who are different from them.
three.what_is_this_world: The soil, the coral reefs and the green cover of the land were built by partners over hundreds of millions of years. Fungi and plants made the first soils together.

roots.thread: Every partnership in this lesson starts from one supply of food: sugar made from sunlight. The alga, the leaf and the flower make it. The fungus, the bee and the coral animal cannot, so each brings something else in exchange. In this way one supply of sugar passes through many very different bodies, and each body adds what the others lack. Long ago, some partners joined so closely that they became one cell. Every plant and every animal is built of such cells.

practice.title: Trade a breath with a plant
practice.say: Sit beside a potted plant, close enough to touch a leaf. Breathe out slowly towards the leaves. Your breath carries carbon dioxide, a gas the plant uses to make sugar. Now breathe in slowly. The oxygen in this air was made by plants, algae and some bacteria. Do this five times. Each time, think of what you give as you breathe out. Think of what you receive as you breathe in. Then sit quietly for a moment. Did either of you have to agree to this exchange?

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through but not tried at home. The Crowded Cup Test (core) needs only cups, soil, kitchen methi and a window. Methi usually comes up in 3 to 4 days. In the first week the three cups look alike, because each seedling lives on the food in the seed. The step says so, and says to go on to day 21 if day 14 shows little. The surest sign is the soil: the cup with 64 seedlings dries out first on the same water. Crowded seedlings are often as tall as the others or taller, but thinner and leaning, so the test compares stems and leaves, not only height. Old methi may sprout poorly. If fewer than half come up, start again with a fresh packet. Lichen from the Spice Box (core) needs kalpasi, which costs little at most grocery shops, and a kitchen scale. Without a scale, compare by bending the wet pieces. How much water the dried spice takes up was not measured by us, so the example numbers are marked as made up. The Lichen Walk and Honest Visitor or Robber? need trees or flowers and are outside the core path. In the middle of a big city the walk may find no lichens, and the step treats that as a result. Pay or Cheat? was played through on paper with 2 players. Nobody can run out of chana in 8 rounds, and the bank of 50 is enough. Two Kinds in One Cup has no fixed answer, and says so.
